title: How Howard Carter Discovered King Tut's Golden Tomb
notes: Cited for: Carnarvon agreed to fund one final season; digging began 1 November 1922; "Yes, wonderful things" in Carter's popular account versus his journal.

title: Discovery of a big void in Khufu's Pyramid by observation of cosmic-ray muons
notes: Cited for: muons from cosmic rays partly absorbed by stone; a big void at least 30 m long above the Grand Gallery; the first major inner structure found since the 19th century.

title: Precise characterization of a corridor-shaped structure in Khufu's Pyramid by observation of cosmic-ray muons
notes: Cited for: a corridor about 9 m long behind the north face, located with muons (2023) and confirmed with an endoscope.

title: Pharaoh Amenhotep I's mummy digitally unwrapped for the first time
notes: Cited for: the mummy never opened in modern times because of its perfect wrappings, garlands and mask; 2021 CT study by Sahar Saleem (Cairo University) and Zahi Hawass; about 35 years old, good teeth, 30 amulets.

title: Space Archaeologist Sarah Parcak Uses Satellites to Uncover Ancient Egyptian Ruins
notes: Cited for: University of Alabama at Birmingham; infrared satellite images show moisture differences above buried mud bricks; Tanis street grid; looting map after 2011.

title: Egyptians call on British Museum to return the Rosetta Stone
notes: Cited for: Hawass petition over 100,000 signatures; British Museum cites the 1801 treaty signed by a representative of Egypt (an Ottoman admiral), no formal request from Egypt, 21 of 28 known copies of the decree in Egypt.

title: ‘Return Rosetta Stone to Egypt’ demands country’s leading archaeologist Zahi Hawass
notes: Cited for: Hawass calls for the return of the Rosetta Stone, the bust of Nefertiti (Berlin) and the Dendera Zodiac (Louvre), saying their home should be in Egypt.

title: Egyptian archaeologist urges German museum to return Nefertiti's bust
notes: Cited for: Hawass's 2024 petition saying the bust, found in 1912 and taken to Berlin in 1913, left Egypt illegally; displayed at the Neues Museum.

title: The Find: Where was the bust of Nefertiti found?
notes: Cited for: found 6 December 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt's excavation at Amarna; official division of finds on 20 January 1913 under the Egyptian antiquities inspector Gustave Lefebvre.

title: Grand Egyptian Museum
notes: Cited for: officially opened 1 November 2025 near the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza; about 100,000 artifacts; the entire Tutankhamun collection shown together for the first time since its discovery.

title: What evidence suggests that the builders of the Great Pyramid of Giza were paid laborers rather than enslaved people?
notes: Cited for: workers' districts with bakeries and workshops; tombs of workers and artisans, some naming the dead.

title: Who Built the Pyramids of Giza?
notes: Cited for: the slave myth traced to Herodotus, misreadings of Exodus and Hollywood films; most archaeologists think paid laborers built the Giza pyramids; workers buried in tombs close to the pyramids.

title: The World's Oldest Papyrus and What It Can Tell Us About the Great Pyramids
notes: Cited for: papyri found at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea in 2013, the oldest known inscribed papyri; Merer's logbook of limestone shipped from Tura to Giza for Khufu, in half-day entries.

title: Plutarch, Life of Antony (Loeb translation, LacusCurtius)
notes: Cited for: chapter 27, Cleopatra's beauty "not altogether incomparable" but converse with her had "an irresistible charm".

title: A (letter)
notes: Cited for: the letter A goes back to a symbol like an ox's head, used in early Semitic writing in Sinai about 1500 BCE, the Phoenician aleph ("ox"), the Greek alpha and Latin.

title: Alphabet (writing)
notes: Cited for: the alphabet's inventors were influenced by Egyptian writing; the proto-Sinaitic inscriptions are a stage between Egyptian hieroglyphs and the North Semitic alphabet.

title: Papyrus (writing material)
notes: Cited for: the word paper derives from papyrus; adopted by the Greeks and used extensively in the Roman Empire; used sporadically until about the 12th century.

title: The Gender Politics Behind Why We're "Mammals"
notes: Cited for: Linnaeus coined Mammalia in 1758, from the Latin mamma, the milk-producing breast; mammals share hair, three middle ear bones and mammary glands.

title: Mammal
notes: Cited for: young nourished with milk from mammary glands; hair typical, but in many whales present only in the fetal stage; three middle ear bones; marsupial newborns continue developing outside the womb.

title: Marine mammals
notes: Cited for: mammals breathe air through lungs, are warm-blooded, have hair at some point in life and produce milk to nurse their young; cetaceans split into baleen and toothed whales.

title: ASM Mammal Diversity Database
notes: Cited for: version 2.5 (released July 28, 2026) lists 6,904 species, of which 6,791 are extant and 113 recently extinct.

title: Lion
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: lions are the most social felines, living in prides of related females (several to 40 animals) with cubs and resident males; females are the primary hunters; roars heard up to five miles away.

title: Tiger
notes: Cited for: the tiger is the largest member of the cat family; tigers are solitary and keep territories.

title: Sumatran tiger
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: tigers in the wild are solitary except when mating or raising young.

title: Elephant
notes: Cited for: three living species (African savanna, African forest, Asian); largest living land animal; trunk combines upper lip and nose with about 150,000 muscle fascicles; gestation up to 22 months, longest of any mammal.

title: Asian elephant
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: the trunk is a fusion of nose and upper lip, contains no bones, and has about 150,000 muscle units.

title: African elephant
notes: Cited for: largest land animals; trunk used for smelling, breathing, trumpeting, drinking and grabbing; female-led herds under a matriarch, usually the biggest and oldest; bulls roam alone or in loose groups; pregnancy almost 22 months.

title: Friend or Foe? Old Elephants Know
notes: Cited for: McComb and colleagues (Science, April 2001) played recorded calls to Amboseli elephant families; families led by matriarchs aged 55 or more discriminated strangers from familiar callers far better and produced more calves.

title: Cetacean
notes: Cited for: cetaceans breathe air, give birth to live young, produce milk and have hair; baleen whales (Mysticeti) and toothed whales (Odontoceti), which include dolphins and porpoises; baleen plates in place of teeth.

title: Cetaceans
notes: Cited for: toothed whales have one blowhole opening and include porpoises and dolphins; baleen whales have two blowholes and baleen plates of keratin that strain small prey; blowholes are nostrils on top of the head.

title: Dolphins Sleep With Only Half Their Brain at a Time
notes: Cited for: dolphins sleep with only half of the brain at a time (unihemispheric sleep), thought to let them breathe at the surface even while asleep.

title: Common Bottlenose Dolphin
notes: Cited for: females are pregnant for about 12 months; calves nurse for about 20 months and stay with their mothers for 3 to 6 years.

title: Species We Study: Bats
notes: Cited for: more than 1,300 bat species; bats make up one-fifth of all mammal species; no other mammal has achieved sustained flight; many rely on echolocation.

title: How Bats Fly
notes: Cited for: bats are the only mammals capable of true flight; the wing resembles a modified hand with the skin between the fingers larger, thinner and stretched; Chiroptera means hand wing.

title: Echolocation
notes: Cited for: bat calls bounce off objects and return to the bats' ears; most are ultrasound, above human hearing; on detecting an insect a bat makes a rapid series of calls to pinpoint it.

title: Marsupial
notes: Cited for: young born in an embryonic condition make their own way to the pouch; the pouch is not universal; most species live in Australia, New Guinea and nearby islands, the rest in the Americas; the red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial.

title: Red Kangaroo
notes: Cited for: newborn is the size of a jellybean and climbs into the pouch after a gestation of around 33 days; joey leaves the pouch at around 235 days and suckles until 12 months.

title: Virginia opossum
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: the only marsupial found north of Mexico; gestation 12 to 13 days; young about 14 mm long climb into the pouch after birth.

title: The platypus puzzle
notes: Cited for: when the first skin reached Europe some suspected a hoax (a duck's bill on a mole's body); George Shaw described it in 1799; monotremes are the platypus and four living echidna species, egg-laying mammals that produce milk.

title: Platypus
notes: Cited for: a unique Australian species; monotremes are distinguished from all other mammals because they lay eggs; young suckle milk from two fur-covered milk patches on the female's abdomen.

title: Platypus
notes: Cited for: one of only two kinds of mammal (with the echidna) that lay eggs; one or two eggs kept warm between body and tail hatch in about ten days.

title: Short-beaked Echidna
notes: Cited for: lays one egg at a time, hatching after about 10 days; the young suckles in the pouch for two or three months until too prickly, then is moved to a burrow; the long-beaked echidna is from New Guinea.

title: Primate
notes: Cited for: primates' eyes face forward with overlapping fields; only primates have flat nails; the primate brain is large for body weight compared with other land mammals.

title: Ape
notes: Cited for: apes are tailless primates, unlike most monkeys; great apes are gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and orangutans; humans share the family Hominidae.

title: Genetics
publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
notes: Cited for: chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives (about 1.2% DNA difference); gorillas about 1.6%; rhesus monkeys about 7%; humans did not evolve from any living primate; human and chimpanzee lineages split 8 to 6 million years ago.

title: Ice Age wolf DNA reveals dogs trace ancestry to two separate wolf populations
notes: Cited for: dogs originated from the gray wolf during the Ice Age, at least 15,000 years ago; where, and whether once or more, is unknown; 72 ancient wolf genomes; dogs closer to ancient eastern wolves, with an eastern source for all dogs and a western source for some.

title: Genomes of modern dogs and wolves provide new insights on domestication
notes: Cited for: dogs and wolves evolved from a common ancestor 9,000 to 34,000 years ago (PLoS Genetics, 2014); dogs are related to something more ancient that isn't well represented by today's wolves.

title: Prehistoric Puppy Was Likely Pet Dog, Archaeologists Say
notes: Cited for: about 14,000 years ago a puppy was buried with a man and a woman; it caught canine distemper at about 19 weeks, died at about 28 weeks, and likely survived only with intensive human care; earliest known evidence of dogs treated as pets.

title: Placental mammal
notes: Cited for: the placenta exchanges nutrients and wastes between the blood of mother and fetus; placentals include all living mammals except marsupials and monotremes.

title: Bird
notes: Cited for: feathers are the major characteristic that distinguishes birds from all other animals; birds lay hard-shelled eggs; in the largest flying birds part of the bone is replaced by air cavities (pneumatic skeleton); not all birds can fly.

title: Bird: Flight
notes: Cited for: a bird's wing acts as both wing and propeller; the basal part of the wing supplies most of the supporting surface, the wing tip most of the propelling force.

title: Beak
notes: Cited for: a bird's bill is the upper and lower jaws covered by a horny sheath; many beaked animals, including all birds and turtles, lack teeth.

title: Adaptations for Flight (Birds of Stanford essays, from The Birder's Handbook)
notes: Cited for: major wing bones have internal strut-like reinforcements that keep their walls from buckling; the skeleton of a frigatebird with a seven-foot wingspan weighs less than its feathers.

title: Brood Patches (Birds of Stanford essays, from The Birder's Handbook)
notes: Cited for: brood patches are belly skin that loses its feathers toward the end of egg-laying and gains extra blood vessels bringing hot blood to the surface; if both parents incubate, both may grow one.

title: Keel (bird anatomy)
notes: Cited for: flying birds have a keel, a ridge on the sternum (breastbone) that is a main site of attachment for flight muscles.

title: Muscle function in avian flight: achieving power and control (Biewener, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2011)
publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
notes: Cited for: birds power flight mainly with large pectoralis muscles that depress the wings; the smaller supracoracoideus, about one-fifth the size of the pectoralis, is the main wing elevator on the upstroke.

title: Nest
notes: Cited for: bird nests range from no real structure (falcons, owls, many seabirds and shorebirds) to woven weaver nests; materials include twigs, leaves, mud, feathers and spiderwebs, with saliva as cement in swifts; sizes from about 2 cm (small hummingbirds) to more than 2 m (large eagles), weights from a few grams to more than a ton.

title: Incubation
notes: Cited for: incubating birds develop a highly vascularised brood patch on breast and belly; ideal incubation temperature for most birds is around 38 °C, adjusted by raising or lowering the body; adults turn the eggs.

title: The Art of Hatching an Egg, Explained (Tim Birkhead, 2016)
notes: Cited for: the egg tooth at the tip of the bill, whose role in hatching William Yarrell discovered in 1826, makes the first hole (pipping); in most birds it falls off a few days after hatching, in passerines it is absorbed into the bill.

title: Bird of prey
notes: Cited for: all birds of prey have hook-tipped beaks and talons; diurnal birds of prey (hawks, eagles, vultures, falcons) are called raptors; owls are the nocturnal birds of prey.

title: Curved beaks
notes: Cited for: falcon beaks have a tomial tooth, a sharp triangular ridge on the upper mandible, used to kill prey by biting the neck; falcons still catch prey with their feet.

title: Neck-breaking, disembowelling, constricting and fishing: the violent world of raptors (on Fowler et al. 2009)
notes: Cited for: accipitrids (eagles, hawks and relatives) have weaker bites and no 'teeth', and use their feet to constrict prey, with two unusually massive talons; falcons use the tomial tooth to kill.

title: Falling with the Falcon (Tom Harpole, Air & Space, March 2005)
notes: Cited for: Ken Franklin's trained peregrine Frightful was clocked at 242 mph stooping from nearly three miles up in 1999 dives filmed for National Geographic, measured with a small chip on her tail feathers; some falcon experts called the setup artificial.

title: Fastest bird (diving)
notes: Cited for: in 1999 the peregrine Frightful, owned by falconer Ken Franklin, was reportedly clocked at 242 mph (389.46 km/h) stooping from about 3 miles up.

title: Peregrine Falcon (Audubon Guide to North American Birds)
notes: Cited for: in power-diving from great heights to strike prey, the peregrine may possibly reach 200 mph.

title: How the owl tracks its prey II (Masakazu Konishi, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2010)
notes: Cited for: Payne and Drury (1958) showed a barn owl could locate mice by sound in total darkness; the owl struck a crumpled wad of paper towed by a mouse, ruling out vision and smell; asymmetrical ears let the owl use level differences to find a sound's elevation.

title: 10 Fun Facts About the American Barn Owl (Anna Gibbs, 2025)
notes: Cited for: barn owls have the greatest ability of any animal tested to locate prey by ear; ears asymmetrical, one slightly above the other; all owls have a facial disc and the barn owl's heart-shaped disc funnels sound to the ears like a satellite dish.

title: The Silent Flight of Owls, Explained (Lesley Evans Ogden, 2017)
notes: Cited for: comb-like serrations on the leading edge, a velvety texture and a soft trailing fringe damp the sound of owl flight; silent flight may keep prey from hearing owls (stealthy hunting hypothesis) and help owls hear prey (prey detection hypothesis).

title: Penguin
notes: Cited for: penguin wings evolved into flippers for underwater propulsion; dense layer of short stiff waterproof feathers and a thick fat layer; countercurrent heat exchange in legs and feet; huddling to share heat; emperor penguins dive to about 550 m, the deepest-diving birds.

title: Bone histology in extant and fossil penguins (Ksepka et al., Journal of Anatomy, 2015)
notes: Cited for: penguin limb bones differ from nearly all other birds' in greater bone density and near complete lack of pneumatization; dense bone is commonly interpreted as reducing buoyancy and conserving energy in diving.

title: Emperor penguin
notes: Cited for: emperor penguins breed during the coldest, darkest winter months; the male incubates for 9 weeks without eating, relying on a thick fat reserve.

title: Hummingbirds
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: a ruby-throated hummingbird's heart beats from 225 a minute at rest to more than 1,200 in flight; wings about 70 beats a second in direct flight, over 200 diving; the only vertebrates capable of sustained hovering, can fly backward and upside down; weigh 2 to 20 grams; poor insulation and high metabolic demands; torpor. Page undated.

title: Hummingbird Hearts Beat 10 Times Faster Than Yours (BirdNote, 2021)
notes: Cited for: an active hummingbird's heart pumps at 1,200 beats per minute, while a human athlete exercising reaches only about 150.

title: Extreme and variable torpor among high-elevation Andean hummingbird species (Wolf et al., Biology Letters, 2020)
notes: Cited for: a black metaltail (Metallura phoebe) in the Peruvian Andes reached a minimum body temperature of 3.26 °C in torpor, the lowest yet reported for any bird or non-hibernating mammal.

title: Manufacture and use of hook-tools by New Caledonian crows (Gavin Hunt, Nature, 1996)
notes: Cited for: wild New Caledonian crows make and use two kinds of hook tool, hooked twigs and stepped-cut barbed pandanus leaves, to catch prey; the tools show a high degree of standardization and distinct tool types.

title: Tool use: New Caledonian crows (Behavioural Ecology Research Group)
publisher: University of Oxford, Behavioural Ecology Research Group
notes: Cited for: New Caledonian crows use tools to forage for invertebrates in dead wood, including tools cut from the thorny edges of pandanus leaves.

title: Tool manufacture: Betty the crow (Behavioural Ecology Research Group; Weir, Chappell and Kacelnik, Science 2002)
publisher: University of Oxford, Behavioural Ecology Research Group
notes: Cited for: after Abel removed the hooked wire, Betty bent a straight wire into a hook and used it to lift a small bucket of meat from a transparent well; only the crows' fifth experience with wire; reported in Weir et al. 2002.

title: Alex, The Renowned African Grey Parrot, Dies At 31 (Brandeis University release, 2007)
notes: Cited for: Alex, studied by Irene Pepperberg for about 30 years, learned to identify 50 objects, 7 colors, 5 shapes, quantities up to 6 and a zero-like concept; died 6 September 2007 at 31.

title: Birds have primate-like numbers of neurons in the forebrain (Olkowicz et al., PNAS, 2016)
notes: Cited for: in 28 bird species, parrot and songbird brains held on average about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass; large-brained parrots and corvids have forebrain neuron counts equal to or greater than primates with much larger brains.

title: Juvenile Bar-tailed Godwit B6 Sets World Record
notes: Cited for: juvenile godwit B6 left Alaska on 13 October 2022 after fattening up on the Kuskokwim Delta and flew nonstop 8,425 miles to Tasmania in 11 days, tracked by a 5-gram solar satellite transmitter; longest documented nonstop flight by any animal.

title: Longest non-stop migration by a bird
notes: Cited for: about 13,560 km (8,425 miles) nonstop by a satellite-tagged juvenile bar-tailed godwit from Alaska to Tasmania, October 2022.

title: How Birds Perform Amazing Migratory Feats, and the Mysteries That Remain (Jillian Mock, 2022)
notes: Cited for: birds sense direction from the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field; some species double their body weight before migrating by gorging on berries, insects or mollusks.

title: Tracking of Arctic terns Sterna paradisaea reveals longest animal migration (Egevang et al., PNAS, 2010)
notes: Cited for: 11 Arctic terns from Greenland and Iceland carrying 1.4-g geolocators flew an average 70,900 km a year on migration (range 59,500 to 81,600 km), with a North Atlantic stopover and wintering in the Southern Ocean; longest round-trip migration recorded electronically; lifetime over 2.4 million km, about three return trips to the Moon, as terns live more than 30 years.

title: Arctic Terns (Newcastle University press release, June 2016)
notes: Cited for: one geolocator-tagged Arctic tern from the Farne Islands, Northumberland, made an estimated 96,000 km round trip to the Weddell Sea, Antarctica (2015 to 2016), for BBC Springwatch.

title: Ostrich
notes: Cited for: largest living bird, flightless, of open country in Africa; adult male up to 2.75 m and more than 150 kg; a frightened ostrich can run 72.5 km/h (45 mph); the only two-toed bird; its egg, averaging about 150 mm long, is the world's largest.

title: Ratite
notes: Cited for: ratites (ostrich, emu, cassowary, rhea, kiwi) have a smooth, raftlike sternum lacking a keel to anchor flight muscles, so they cannot fly.

title: Biology 2e, 29.4 Reptiles
notes: Cited for: reptiles' scaly skin, containing keratin and waxy lipids, reduces water loss; the amnion gives the embryo its own internal aquatic environment and shells retain water and nutrients; Crocodilia include alligators, crocodiles, gharials and caimans.

title: Reptile
notes: Cited for: most reptiles have a continuous covering of epidermal scales whose main component is keratin; embryos develop in an amnion, usually in shelled eggs; living groups are turtles, tuatara, lizards and snakes, and crocodiles, over 12,500 species; most are ectothermic.

title: Keratin
notes: Cited for: keratin is the fibrous structural protein of hair, nails, horn, hoofs, wool, feathers and the outer layers of the skin.

title: Reptilia
publisher: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology)
notes: Cited for: reptile eggs are protected from drying by the amnion and covered with a leathery or calcium-based shell, partly or wholly lost in species that give birth to live young.

title: The Amniotic Egg
notes: Cited for: the amniotic egg freed early vertebrates from dependence on water for reproduction; most amphibians lay soft, gelatinous eggs in aquatic environments; many reptiles lay leathery-shelled eggs in nests.

title: Snake
notes: Cited for: snakes differ from other reptiles in being limbless with a greatly elongated body and tail; they lack movable eyelids and external ear openings.

title: Snake: Locomotion
notes: Cited for: the four ways snakes move (serpentine, concertina, rectilinear, sidewinding); serpentine loops push against rocks, twigs and pebbles; heavy-bodied snakes such as boas use rectilinear movement, pushing with ventral scales.

title: Why Do Snakes Flick Their Tongues?
notes: Cited for: a flicking tongue captures scent particles and carries them to the Jacobson's organ on the roof of the mouth; each tip of the fork samples a different point, giving directional ('stereo') smell.

title: UC study explains how Burmese pythons can eat deer, other big prey
notes: Cited for: unlike ours, snakes' lower jawbones are not connected, letting them open wide; stretchy skin adds to the gape; a wild Burmese python in Everglades National Park regurgitated an adult white-tailed deer (Bruce Jayne, 2022).

title: Snakes
notes: Cited for: a stretchy ligament lets a snake open its mouth very wide and move both jaws independently; snakes swallow prey much larger than their heads by 'walking' their mouth around it.

title: Venom
notes: Cited for: venom is produced by specialized glands and must be injected by a bite or sting, while poisons harm when ingested or absorbed through the skin; venoms are mixtures of toxic enzymes and other proteins; neurotoxins act on the nervous system, hemotoxins on blood and blood vessels.

title: What's the difference between a poisonous and venomous animal?
notes: Cited for: venomous animals deliver toxins by wounding, via a fang, stinger or spine; poisonous organisms deliver them passively when touched or eaten, as poison frogs and pufferfishes do.

title: Snakebite envenoming (fact sheet)
notes: Cited for: around 81,410 to 137,880 people die each year from snakebites; venom can cause paralysis that prevents breathing and bleeding disorders; antivenoms are the most effective treatment and most deaths are preventable.

title: Antivenom: a brief history
publisher: Fogarty International Center, U.S. National Institutes of Health
notes: Cited for: Albert Calmette created the first snake antivenom (anti-cobra serum, 1894) and began producing it in horses at the Pasteur Institute in Lille in 1895; most antivenoms are still made in horses, some in sheep, by injecting small amounts of venom and harvesting the antibodies.

title: Turtle
notes: Cited for: the carapace and plastron join into a rigid skeletal box the turtle cannot exit or shed; about 356 species on every continent except Antarctica; all tortoises are turtles, and tortoises live only on land.

title: Turtle: Form and function
notes: Cited for: the carapace consists of 10 trunk vertebrae and their ribs, overlain by and fused to dermal plates.

title: What causes a sea turtle to be born male or female?
notes: Cited for: sea turtle eggs incubated below 27.7 °C hatch male, above 31 °C female, and in between a mix.

title: Rising Temperatures Turning Major Sea Turtle Population Female
notes: Cited for: a study published January 2018 found that green turtles from the warmer northern Great Barrier Reef beaches were 99.1 percent female among juveniles and 99.8 percent among subadults.

title: Crocodile
notes: Cited for: crocodiles have a narrow, V-shaped snout and some lower teeth visible with the mouth closed, while alligators have a broad, U-shaped snout; eyes, ears and nostrils stay above water while the body is submerged.

title: American alligator
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: the alligator's large fourth lower tooth fits into a socket in the upper jaw and is hidden when the mouth is closed, unlike in crocodiles; alligators live mostly in fresh water and tolerate salt water only briefly because they lack salt glands.

title: Salt Glands in the Tongue of the Estuarine Crocodile Crocodylus porosus (Science, 1981)
notes: Cited for: Taplin and Grigg identified salt-secreting glands in the tongue of the estuarine (saltwater) crocodile.

title: Saltwater crocodile
notes: Cited for: the saltwater or estuarine crocodile is the largest living crocodilian, growing to 23 feet; it is a skilled swimmer, sometimes seen far out at sea.

title: Chameleon
notes: Cited for: chameleons are Old World lizards best known for changing colour; it is a popular misconception that they change colour to match the background; colour change responds to light, temperature and emotional states, and striking colours appear in males during mating.

title: The chameleon reorganizes its nanocrystals to change colors
notes: Cited for: 2015 UNIGE study of panther chameleons: colour change by active tuning of a lattice of nanocrystals in iridophores; calm, a dense lattice reflects blue; excited, a loosened lattice reflects yellows and reds; males change within a minute or two to court or face rivals; a deeper layer reflects infrared, protecting against heat.

title: Photonic crystals cause active colour change in chameleons (Nature Communications, 2015)
notes: Cited for: Teyssier, Saenko, van der Marel and Milinkovitch show panther chameleons shift colour by tuning a lattice of guanine nanocrystals during male contests and courtship; many vertebrates instead change colour by moving pigment-containing organelles.

title: Chameleons' Craziest Color Changes Aren't for Camouflage
notes: Cited for: chameleons' dramatic colour changes are social signals; as ectotherms they can turn darker to absorb more light and warm up faster; their camouflage repertoire is limited.

title: Biology 2e, 29.3 Amphibians
notes: Cited for: 'amphibian' loosely means 'dual life'; moist, permeable skin through which most water is taken in and which is one of three respiratory surfaces; three groups (salamanders, frogs, caecilians); tadpoles have gills and long finned tails, lack limbs and are often herbivores.

title: Global Amphibian Assessment 2
notes: Cited for: the second Global Amphibian Assessment (published 2023) found 41% of 8,011 assessed amphibian species threatened, more than mammals, birds or reptiles; disease (chytridiomycosis) was the leading cause of worsening risk 1980 to 2004, climate change since 2004.

title: Mass amphibian extinctions globally caused by fungal disease
notes: Cited for: Scheele and colleagues (Science, 2019) found chytrid fungus disease, which eats away at amphibian skin, drove declines in over 500 species, including 90 extinctions, over the past 50 years.

title: Amphibian fungal panzootic causes catastrophic and ongoing loss of biodiversity (Science, 2019)
notes: Cited for: chytridiomycosis contributed to the decline of at least 501 amphibian species over the past half-century, including 90 presumed extinctions.

title: Pathogenesis of Chytridiomycosis, a Cause of Catastrophic Amphibian Declines (Science, 2009)
notes: Cited for: Voyles and colleagues showed the chytrid skin infection disrupts electrolyte transport across the skin, lowering blood salts until the heart stops.

title: Frog
notes: Cited for: during metamorphosis the lungs develop, limbs appear, the tail is absorbed and the mouth becomes froglike; the tadpole becomes a frog within two months to three years.

title: Frogs: The Amazing, Adaptable Frog
notes: Cited for: metamorphosis begins as the hind legs sprout; lungs develop and the front legs appear; the tail gradually shrinks; the gills disappear just before the tadpole becomes a frog.

title: Functions and Mechanism of Thyroid Hormone Receptor Action During Amphibian Development (Endocrinology, 2024)
notes: Cited for: in 1912 Friedrich Gudernatsch fed tadpoles several horse organs and only the thyroid accelerated metamorphosis; removing a tadpole's thyroid stopped metamorphosis.

title: Dinosaur
notes: Cited for: dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles; the name comes from Greek deinos ('terrible' or 'fearfully great') and sauros ('reptile' or 'lizard'); Owen proposed Dinosauria in 1842; Buckland described Megalosaurus in 1824 mainly from a lower jaw; dinosaurs held their limbs under the body like elephants, not sprawled like lizards.

title: Why Aren't Pterosaurs Dinosaurs?
publisher: Natural History Museum of Utah (University of Utah)
notes: Cited for: dinosaurs evolved separately from flying reptiles; dinosaurs have a hole in the hip socket, while pterosaurs' sockets are a bony depression; marine reptiles are lineages that evolved separately from dinosaurs.

title: Maiasaura
notes: Cited for: in 1978 a Maiasaura nesting site near Choteau, Montana, yielded nests with clutches of eggs, broken eggshells and juveniles; embryo bones not fully ossified imply parental care.

title: Paleontology: Egg Mountain (Montana Geoheritage)
publisher: Science Education Resource Center, Carleton College
notes: Cited for: Jack Horner and Bob Makela identified baby duck-billed dinosaur bones and the first nest with hatchlings; Maiasaura means 'good mother lizard'; babies unable to walk had worn teeth, suggesting parents fed them.

title: Amphibians (Great Smoky Mountains National Park)
notes: Cited for: salamanders have smooth, moist skin and eggs in clear jelly, lizards dry scaly skin and leathery-shelled eggs; the park has more salamander species than anywhere on Earth, 31, including 25 lungless salamanders that breathe through their skin and mouth and throat linings.

title: Mistaken Identities: Lizards vs. Salamanders
notes: Cited for: lizards have dry scaly skin, claws on their toes and ear openings; salamanders have moist, permeable skin, no claws and no ear openings.

title: Fish
notes: Cited for: scales of bony fishes are thin overlapping plates of bone that grow throughout life; most fish are cold-blooded, but the opah is warm-blooded through a heat exchange system in its gills.

title: How Do Fish Breathe?
notes: Cited for: fish breathe through gills that extract dissolved oxygen from water; water flows over blood-rich gill filaments, oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves.

title: Pectoral fin
notes: Cited for: pectoral fins are paired fins crucial for stabilization and steering, working with the dorsal and caudal fins to keep balance.

title: Shark
notes: Cited for: sharks are cartilaginous fishes.

title: Fun Facts About Shocking Sharks
notes: Cited for: sharks have no bones, only cartilage; sharks have eight senses (hearing, smell, lateral line, pit organs, vision, ampullae of Lorenzini, touch, taste).

title: Sharks: bodies and senses
notes: Cited for: shark cartilage is lightweight and flexible, like the human ear; sharks have an acute sense of smell; the lateral line is a row of pores whose sensory cells detect pressure changes.

title: Respect: Sharks are Older than Trees
notes: Cited for: sharks have been around for about 400 million years; the earliest trees, such as Archaeopteris, lived around 350 million years ago.

title: Yearly Worldwide Shark Attack Summary (ISAF 2025 report)
publisher: Florida Museum of Natural History, International Shark Attack File
notes: Cited for: 65 confirmed unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, in line with the 2020 to 2024 average of 61 a year; the total remains extremely low.

title: How far does light travel in the ocean?
notes: Cited for: light may be detected as far as 1,000 meters down but rarely significantly beyond 200 meters; below 1,000 meters sunlight does not penetrate.

title: Fishes of the Midnight Zone
notes: Cited for: darkness, pressure, cold and distance from the plankton base of the food chain limit deep-sea life; female anglerfishes carry a lure (esca) lit by bioluminescent bacteria; backward-pointing teeth.

title: New study shows that three quarters of deep-sea animals make their own light
notes: Cited for: 2017 study by Severine Martini and Steve Haddock: three quarters of animals in Monterey Bay waters from the surface to 4,000 meters can produce light.

title: Ten Wild Facts About Octopuses
notes: Cited for: three hearts (two for the gills, one for the body, which stops when swimming); blue copper-based hemocyanin blood; two thirds of neurons in the arms; problem solving, mazes and memory.

title: Octopuses keep surprising us: here are eight examples how
notes: Cited for: the common octopus has about 500 million neurons, about as many as a dog, about two thirds in its arms; blue haemocyanin blood contains copper.

title: What are jellyfish made of?
notes: Cited for: jellyfish are about 95 percent water; they lack brains, blood and hearts and use a nerve net; one opening serves as mouth and anus.

title: How Jellyfish Rule the Seas Without a Brain
notes: Cited for: nematocysts are capsules with coiled harpoons; hundreds fire in jabs lasting about 700 nanoseconds, with force enough to pierce a crustacean shell.

title: Sockeye Salmon
notes: Cited for: sockeye hatch in fresh water, spend 1 to 3 years there, migrate to sea for 2 to 3 years and return to spawn, usually where they were born; they turn bright red and all die within weeks of spawning; bears and eagles eat them; carcasses nourish the river and young salmon.

title: Fish Olfaction and Homing Research
notes: Cited for: juvenile salmon imprint on the odors of their natal stream before migrating to sea, and adults use those odor memories to home.

title: How Salmon Find Their Way
publisher: Alaska Department of Fish and Game
notes: Cited for: salmon imprint on the smells of their surroundings and on the Earth's magnetic field where they first enter the sea.

title: What is the intertidal zone?
notes: Cited for: the intertidal zone lies between high and low tides; tides flood and drain the middle zone twice a day, home to sea stars and anemones; animals close up in shells or retreat to stay wet; hermit crabs reuse empty shells.

title: Are starfish really fish?
notes: Cited for: sea stars are not fish (no gills, scales or fins); they move and hold prey with tube feet and can regrow lost arms.

title: Sea star
notes: Cited for: sea stars force open bivalve shells with their suction feet, insert the stomach and digest the prey.

title: What are plankton?
notes: Cited for: plankton are drifters carried by tides and currents (Greek for drifter); phytoplankton and zooplankton; zooplankton include krill, young fish and jellyfish; phytoplankton photosynthesize near the surface; nightly vertical migration is considered the largest on Earth.

title: How much oxygen comes from the ocean?
notes: Cited for: roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from photosynthesizing plankton; marine life consumes about the same amount.

title: Numbers of Insects (Species and Individuals)
notes: Cited for: an estimated 10 quintillion individual insects alive at any time; the largest insect orders are beetles, flies, ants/bees/wasps and moths/butterflies.

title: Insect
notes: Cited for: the insect body in three regions (head with a pair of antennae, thorax with three pairs of legs and usually wings, abdomen); insects have exoskeletons.

title: ENY203/IG080: Ants
notes: Cited for: ant queens reproduce and may live many years; workers are sterile females; males mate and die; some ants lay pheromone scent trails.

title: How Ants Became the World’s Best Fungus Farmers
notes: Cited for: fungus-farming ants gather vegetation to nourish fungi they eat; the crop is not found in the wild; ants farmed about 60 million years before human agriculture.

title: Honeybee
notes: Cited for: enzymes turn nectar into honey; bees beat their wings to evaporate it and seal cells with wax; four pairs of wax glands; comb of six-sided cells; workers are female; pollen baskets.

title: Honey
notes: Cited for: nectar ripens into honey by sugar inversion and removal of moisture; honey is about 18 percent water; stored in beeswax honeycomb.

title: Bulletin #7153, Understanding Native Bees, the Great Pollinators
notes: Cited for: bees have dense branched hairs that collect pollen; a feeding bee may deposit pollen on a flower’s stigma.

title: What is Pollination?
notes: Cited for: pollination is the transfer of pollen from a flower’s anther to its stigma; flowers rely on vectors such as insects to move pollen.

title: The Birds and the Bees
notes: Cited for: pollinators get nectar or pollen as food from flowers, and in return carry pollen from one flower to another.

title: Monarch Butterfly Biology
notes: Cited for: the monarch’s four life stages (egg, larva, pupa, adult) called complete metamorphosis; eggs hatch in about four days; larvae grow from under 1 cm to about 5 cm.

title: How Does a Caterpillar Turn into a Butterfly?
notes: Cited for: inside the chrysalis the caterpillar digests itself into caterpillar soup; imaginal discs grown in the egg survive and build adult parts; a fruit fly wing disc grows from about 50 to more than 50,000 cells.

title: Spider
notes: Cited for: spiders have two body parts and eight legs, no antennae; silk made in abdominal glands leaves through spinnerets; nearly all spiders are predators; not all build webs.

title: Spider webs
notes: Cited for: many nocturnal orb weavers eat their webs toward dawn and rebuild each night; eaten silk protein returns to the silk glands; an orb web takes about 30 to 45 minutes.

title: Gastropod
notes: Cited for: gastropods are the largest group of mollusks; slugs are snails whose shells were reduced or lost in evolution; movement on a muscular foot and a mucus track.

title: Mollusk
notes: Cited for: mollusks are soft-bodied invertebrates, usually in a shell secreted by the mantle; the main groups (snails and slugs, clams and mussels, squids and octopuses).

title: A Microscopic Look at Snail Jaws
publisher: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County
notes: Cited for: snails and slugs eat with a jaw and a radula, a flexible band of thousands of microscopic teeth that rasps food.

title: Mollusks: Diet and Behavior
notes: Cited for: the radula is a membrane with rows of tiny chitin teeth, coarse like sandpaper.

title: Earthworm
notes: Cited for: earthworms lack lungs and breathe through their skin; ringlike segments (up to 150 in L. terrestris); diet of decaying plants plus soil; burrows aerate soil and draw in organic matter.

title: Earthworms
notes: Cited for: burrows create passages for air, water and roots; casts are richer than surrounding soil; earthworms breathe through moist skin; noticed mainly after heavy rain.

title: Vegetable Mould and Worms (editorial introduction by R. B. Freeman)
publisher: The Complete Work of Charles Darwin Online
notes: Cited for: Darwin’s worm book was published on 10 October 1881, sold 6,000 copies within a year and at first sold far faster than On the Origin of Species.

title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms (Charles Darwin, 1881)
notes: Cited for: Darwin’s estimate that more than ten tons of dry earth per acre pass through worms each year in many parts of England, and that worms plowed the land long before people.

title: Crustacean
notes: Cited for: crabs, lobsters, shrimps and wood lice are crustaceans; crustaceans have two pairs of antenna-like appendages in front of the mouth.

title: Arthropod
notes: Cited for: arthropods have a jointed chitin-protein exoskeleton and segmented bodies with paired jointed appendages (name means jointed feet); main groups; about 84 percent of described animal species.

title: Arthropod: Form and function
notes: Cited for: crustacean exoskeletons are stiffened with calcium carbonate; growth by molting; the new soft exoskeleton is stretched with water or air and then hardens.

title: Ecdysis
notes: Cited for: the rigid exoskeleton limits growth, so arthropods shed and replace it periodically; the new cuticle is soft.

title: American Lobster
notes: Cited for: lobsters molt to grow, about 20 to 25 times over 5 to 8 years before they can reproduce, and often eat their old shells to replenish calcium.

title: Crab identification and soft-shelled crab
notes: Cited for: a newly molted soft-shelled crab is extremely vulnerable and hides for a few days; the shell keeps hardening for two to three months.

title: Fighting the World’s Deadliest Animal
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: the CDC calls the mosquito the world’s deadliest animal; mosquitoes spread malaria, dengue, West Nile, Zika, chikungunya and lymphatic filariasis.

title: About Mosquitoes
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: only female mosquitoes bite, needing a blood meal to produce eggs; both sexes feed on nectar and fruit juices; mosquitoes pick up and spread germs by biting.

title: Life Cycle of Anopheles Mosquitoes
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: Anopheles eggs are laid on water; larvae and pupae live in water and pupae do not eat; egg to adult takes 10 to 14 days; adult females bite.

title: Malaria (fact sheet, 4 December 2025)
notes: Cited for: an estimated 282 million malaria cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024; 95 percent of deaths in the WHO African Region, about 75 percent of them children under 5; spread by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes; caused by Plasmodium parasites.

title: Mosquito
notes: Cited for: mosquitoes (family Culicidae) are insects, about 3,500 species, some important to public health because the females suck blood.

title: Adaptation
notes: Cited for: adaptation is the adjustment of organisms to their environment to improve their chances of survival; biological and behavioral adaptations; individuals cannot adapt, only populations.

title: Adaptation (biology and physiology)
notes: Cited for: adaptation is the process by which a species becomes fitted to its environment, the result of natural selection acting on heritable variation over several generations.

title: How Does a Fennec Fox Survive in the Desert? And Other Questions, Answered
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: relative to body size the fennec has the largest ears in the dog family, which help dispel body heat; thick-furred paws protect from hot sand; nocturnal, burrows by day.

title: Arctic Fox
notes: Cited for: Arctic foxes have small ears, which reduce heat loss because less is exposed to the cold.

title: Arctic fox
notes: Cited for: short rounded ears, short muzzle and fur-covered soles as adaptations to the Arctic; the white phase is grayish brown in summer and white in winter.

title: Camouflage
notes: Cited for: background matching (deer, squirrels, flounder, walking sticks, walking leaves that sway like leaves); countershading in sharks; Arctic fox seasonal coat; warning coloration of monarchs; scarlet king snake mimics the coral snake.

title: Countershading
notes: Cited for: countershading gives darker upper surfaces than the lower, unilluminated ones, evening out shading so the body looks flatter and less visible.

title: Mimicry
notes: Cited for: Batesian mimicry, in which a defenseless organism closely resembles a noxious, conspicuous one; described by Henry W. Bates in 1862 from Brazilian butterflies.

title: Müllerian mimicry
notes: Cited for: Fritz Müller proposed in 1878 that inedible species resemble each other; a predator that learns to avoid one pattern avoids similar species; monarchs keep milkweed cardenolides for protection.

title: The viceroy butterfly is not a batesian mimic (Nature 350: 497-498, 1991)
notes: Cited for: Ritland and Brower offered red-winged blackbirds butterfly abdomens without wings; viceroys were as unpalatable as monarchs, so the viceroy is a Müllerian, not Batesian, mimic.

title: Viceroy butterfly Limenitis archippus (EENY-458)
publisher: University of Florida IFAS Extension (Featured Creatures)
notes: Cited for: the viceroy is similar to but smaller than the monarch; long thought a Batesian mimic, it is distasteful too, so the relationship was shown to be Müllerian.

title: Hibernation
notes: Cited for: hibernation is greatly reduced metabolism and lowered body temperature; body temperature near 0 C, a few breaths a minute, heartbeat barely detectable; wakes every several weeks; bears are not considered true hibernators.

title: Explainer: How brief can hibernation be?
notes: Cited for: torpor is a state in which body temperature falls and cells slow; daily torpor lasts a few hours, used by white-footed mice, shrews and some birds.

title: Arctic ground squirrels are supercooled (UAF Centennial)
notes: Cited for: Brian Barnes found in the late 1980s that hibernating Arctic ground squirrels supercool, with core temperatures below freezing, and rewarm every few weeks.

title: Freeze avoidance in a mammal: body temperatures below 0 C in an Arctic hibernator (Science, 1989)
notes: Cited for: hibernating Arctic ground squirrels adopted core body temperatures as low as -2.9 C without freezing.

title: Hibernation in Black Bears: Independence of Metabolic Suppression from Body Temperature (Science, 2011)
notes: Cited for: Toien and colleagues (University of Alaska Fairbanks) found black bears cut metabolism to about 25% of normal while body temperature fell only about 5 to 6 C; 5 to 7 months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating.

title: Do Camels Store Water in Their Humps?
notes: Cited for: humps store fat, a food reserve, and concentrating fat there limits insulation elsewhere; camels drink up to 30 gallons in one sitting and survive nearly a week without drinking.

title: Kangaroo Rat (Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument)
notes: Cited for: kangaroo rats get half a gram of water from each gram of seeds (about one drop per two seeds), have almost no need for liquid water, concentrate urine, forage at night.

title: Dipodomys merriami (Merriam's kangaroo rat)
publisher: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology)
notes: Cited for: neither sweat nor pant; specialized kidneys lose very little water; nocturnal, staying in burrows during the day.

title: Ursus maritimus (polar bear)
publisher: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology)
notes: Cited for: black skin and clear, unpigmented fur that looks white by refracting light; eats seal blubber to keep its insulating fat layer; furred soles for insulation and traction.

title: Polar bear
notes: Cited for: thick fur over black skin; a layer of insulating fat under the skin; hairy soles that insulate and help on ice.

title: How Do Penguins Stay Warm?
notes: Cited for: short, stiff, tightly packed feathers trap air; a thick fat layer; closely aligned arteries and veins in the legs transfer heat from outgoing to returning blood.

title: Penguin: Form and function
notes: Cited for: heat exchange between adjacent arteries and veins in the legs; emperor penguins keep foot skin near 0 C and so do not melt the ice they stand on; plumage air layer gives almost complete insulation.

title: Photo Ark: Southern Three-Banded Armadillo
notes: Cited for: leathery armor plates; rolls completely into a ball; the Brazilian three-banded armadillo is the only other armadillo that can.

title: North American porcupine
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: about 30,000 quills; quills are not thrown but are lightly attached and come off easily; they work deeper into skin at about 1 mm an hour; cornered porcupines raise quills, turn and lash the tail.

title: The Striped Skunk: America's Misunderstood Neighbor
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: warning display before spraying; spray reaches about 10 feet (3 m) with startling accuracy; about a week to replenish; white stripes signal alarm (aposematism).

title: Nocturnal animals, explained
notes: Cited for: nocturnal animals are active after dark to hunt, mate or avoid daytime heat and predators; enlarged eyes with widened pupils collect more light; reflective tapetum.

title: Tapetum lucidum
notes: Cited for: reflective layer behind the retina of many nocturnal vertebrates that reflects light back onto the photoreceptors; causes eyeshine; found in cats, crocodiles, lemurs.

title: Tarsier
notes: Cited for: nocturnal primate with enormous eyes; lacks the reflective tapetum most other nocturnal mammals have.

title: Tarsiidae (tarsiers)
publisher: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology)
notes: Cited for: all tarsiers are nocturnal or crepuscular; one eye weighs nearly as much as the brain.

title: Electroreception
notes: Cited for: sharks and rays detect weak electric fields of prey, even buried in sand, with the ampullae of Lorenzini; humans lack electroreceptors.

title: Pit viper
notes: Cited for: pit vipers, including rattlesnakes, have a heat-sensitive pit organ between each eye and nostril that helps aim strikes at warm-blooded prey.

title: Magnetoreception (Lohmann Lab)
publisher: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
notes: Cited for: sea turtles use Earth's magnetic field to navigate long migrations; loggerhead hatchlings swam in different directions in the magnetic fields of different locations along their route.

title: Reindeer use UV light to survive in the wild (UCL News, May 2011)
notes: Cited for: Glen Jeffery's team (Journal of Experimental Biology, 2011) found reindeer see ultraviolet; lichen, urine and wolf fur absorb UV and appear dark against snow; human lenses block UV.

title: Wildlife's most magical adaptations
notes: Cited for: wood frogs winter in leaf litter and can freeze 65% of their bodies; glucose fills cells so their insides do not freeze while outside water does; hearts stop; they thaw from the inside out, starting with the heart.

title: Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1973
notes: Cited for: Karl von Frisch, Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen shared the 1973 prize for discoveries concerning organization and elicitation of individual and social behaviour patterns; founders of ethology; round dance near the hive, waggle dance farther away, straight run relative to the sun translated to upwards on a vertical comb, polarized light; described the dance as genetically programmed and not learnt; imprinting during an early critical period (duckling follows the first moving object it sees, a mother, a cardboard box or a balloon); Tinbergen tested gull-chick begging with dummies and found supranormal stimuli.

title: Instinct
notes: Cited for: Instinct is an inborn, stereotyped, apparently unlearned, genetically determined behaviour pattern; newly hatched herring gull chicks peck at the red spot on the parent's bill to stimulate regurgitation of food; no behaviour is strictly innate or entirely learned.

title: Biology 2e, 45.7 Behavioral Biology: Proximate and Ultimate Causes of Behavior
notes: Cited for: Innate behaviors have a strong genetic component and carry no risk of being learned incorrectly; learned behaviors are flexible and modified by experience; prairie dogs habituate to human footsteps but still call at predators; imprinting; signal channels (chemical pheromones, sound, visual displays, touch); pheromone uses; aggressive displays reduce fighting and may bluff; peahens choose the brightest males; birdsong identifies species and attracts mates; courtship displays run in steps and are abandoned if a step fails.

title: Konrad Lorenz
notes: Cited for: In 1935 Lorenz imitated a mother duck's quacking before newly hatched mallard ducklings, which then regarded him as their mother; at a critical stage soon after hatching, young birds learn to follow real or foster parents; shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Frisch and Tinbergen.

title: Raising Cranes
notes: Cited for: Costume rearing (costume and hand puppet mimicking an adult crane) makes chicks imprint on Whooping Cranes; Tex, a human-raised female of the 1970s, was bonded with people and would not pair with another Whooping Crane.

title: The Man Who Saves Cranes
notes: Cited for: Tex hatched at the San Antonio Zoo, grew up with humans and imprinted on them; George Archibald danced with her from spring 1976, since dancing is how whooping cranes initiate mating; on June 3, 1982, Tex hatched a chick named Gee Whiz.

title: Animal communication
notes: Cited for: Animal communication is the process by which one animal provides information that other animals can incorporate into their decision making; signals can be sound, colour pattern, posture, movement, electrical discharge, touch or odour.

title: Monkey Responses to Three Different Alarm Calls: Evidence of Predator Classification and Semantic Communication (Science, 1980)
notes: Cited for: Seyfarth, Cheney and Marler: vervet monkeys in Amboseli, Kenya, give acoustically different alarm calls to leopards, eagles and snakes; played back with no predator present, the calls made monkeys run into trees (leopard), look up (eagle) or look down (snake).

title: Karl von Frisch
notes: Cited for: The circling (round) dance indicates food near the hive, the wagging dance a greater distance; bees use the Sun as a compass through their perception of polarized light, even when the Sun is not visible; shared the 1973 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine.

title: Bee Dancing is Better with the Right Audience
notes: Cited for: The angle of the waggle dance conveys the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the duration of the performance encodes the distance to the source.

title: Complex Learned Social Behavior Discovered in Bee's 'Waggle Dance'
notes: Cited for: Dong, Lin, Tan and Nieh (Science, 2023): bees that could not follow experienced dancers before first dancing produced more disordered dances with larger angle errors and encoded distance incorrectly; they improved with practice but never encoded distance correctly.

title: Animal social behaviour: Aggregation and individual protection
notes: Cited for: A group member's chance of being eaten falls from p to p/N when a predator takes one prey per encounter; the interior of a group such as a fish school is safer; groups confuse predators; alarm calls reduce predation; lions, hyenas and wolves that cooperate can corner and bring down prey more easily; if a group attracts too many predators an individual may be better off alone; competition for food.

title: Alpha Status, Dominance, and Division of Labor in Wolf Packs (Mech, 1999)
publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Northern Prairie Wildlife Research Center (University of Nebraska-Lincoln DigitalCommons)
notes: Cited for: Canadian Journal of Zoology 77:1196-1203. Captive packs were assortments of unrelated wolves (Schenkel 1947 and others) that formed alpha, beta, omega hierarchies; a wild pack is usually a family of a breeding pair and their offspring of the previous 1-3 years; in 13 summers observing the Ellesmere Island pack Mech saw no dominance contests; female mainly pup care and defense, male mainly foraging and food provisioning; dominance displays mainly over food, letting parents feed the youngest.

title: Is the Alpha Wolf Idea a Myth?
notes: Cited for: The alpha idea came from mid-20th-century studies of captive packs of unrelated adults; wild packs are families led by a breeding pair; Mech, a USGS senior research scientist, once used alpha and beta himself and now compares an alpha to a human father.

title: Satin Bowerbird
notes: Cited for: The male builds a bower of two parallel walls of sticks on the ground as a courtship arena, decorates it with blue objects (clothes pegs, drinking straws, bottle tops, parrot feathers, flowers), paints it with chewed plant matter and saliva, displays by strutting and bowing with quivering wings and mechanical calls while holding a decoration; the female mates and then nests alone.

title: Animal social behaviour: Costs and benefits of parental care
notes: Cited for: A female guarding a clutch of eggs does so at the expense of laying another clutch; mammal mothers carry young through gestation and provide care through lactation; male-only care is rare, but seahorse and pipefish males carry the eggs and brood the young.

title: Seahorse
notes: Cited for: The female places her eggs in a brood pouch at the base of the male's tail; the eggs stay between 10 days and six weeks; the male expels the young through an opening in the pouch; the young receive no further care.

title: Orangutan
publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
notes: Cited for: Infants cling to their mothers from birth and can nurse until six to seven years old; a female has a baby only about every seven to nine years, four to five in her lifetime; females may stay with their mothers into their teens, watching younger siblings raised.

title: Does Tool Use Define Humanity?
notes: Cited for: Jane Goodall on David Greybeard using a tool at Gombe; chimps stripped leafy twigs of their leaves, object modification never seen before; Louis Leakey replied that we must redefine man or accept chimpanzees as human.

title: Jane Goodall
notes: Cited for: Goodall set up camp in the Gombe Stream Game Reserve (Tanzania) in June 1960 and found that chimpanzees make and use tools; she died October 1, 2025.

title: Otters, Especially Females, Use Tools To Survive a Changing World
publisher: The University of Texas at Austin
notes: Cited for: Law and colleagues (Science, 2024) followed 196 radio-tagged southern sea otters in California; otters use rocks, shells and trash to break open prey; tool users, mostly females, ate harder and larger prey and had less tooth damage; worn teeth can mean starvation; females likely use tools to offset smaller bodies and weaker bites, as raising pups takes a lot of energy.

title: "Bizarre" Octopuses Carry Coconuts as Instant Shelters
notes: Cited for: Julian Finn and colleagues observed veined octopuses (Amphioctopus marginatus) in Indonesia digging up coconut shell halves, carrying them beneath their bodies while walking on stiffened arms and assembling them as shelter; a hermit crab shell is not a tool because it is always useful, while the coconut gives only delayed benefits; first tool use known in an invertebrate (2009).

title: Can Fish Recognize Themselves in the Mirror?
notes: Cited for: The mirror self-recognition test, developed by Gordon Gallup Jr. in 1970: habituation (many attack the reflection), contingency testing, then a colored mark; chimpanzees, dolphins, elephants and corvids seem to pass; 10 cleaner wrasse (PLOS Biology, 2019) scraped marked throats; Gallup suggested they may have been reacting to an apparent parasite.

title: This tiny fish can recognize itself in a mirror. Is it self-aware?
notes: Cited for: Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies have passed the mirror test; Gallup doubted the cleaner wrasse result; the test may not show what we think it does.

title: Happy, an Asian Elephant Who Demonstrated That Her Species Might Be Self-Aware, Dies at 55 at the Bronx Zoo
notes: Cited for: 2006 Bronx Zoo study (Plotnik and colleagues) of three Asian elephants, Happy, Maxine and Patty; Happy repeatedly touched a visible white X on her head, with an invisible sham mark on the other side as a control; only Happy clearly passed.

title: Do Dogs Know Themselves?
notes: Cited for: Dogs are beings of smell, not sight; in Alexandra Horowitz's 2017 olfactory mirror test, dogs spent more time investigating their own urine when an added odor modified it.

title: The evolutionary case for a little roughhousing
notes: Cited for: Play has no apparent immediate function yet costs energy and is noisy and conspicuous; young rats with the advantage often cede it by rolling onto their backs; young elk lock horns in play but never butt heads; play-deprived rats grow up anxious, overreact and are inept at courtship; play-fighting trains the prefrontal cortex to adjust behavior to the situation (Pellis).

title: For a Model of Fair Play, Look to Dogs
notes: Cited for: Bekoff and Pierce: canids solicit play with a bow, crouching on their forelimbs while standing on their hind legs; bows are used almost exclusively in play and are highly stereotyped; after a bow, rough actions draw submission or avoidance only about 15 percent of the time; self-handicapping and role reversal keep play fair.

title: Charles Darwin
notes: Cited for: Darwin born 1809; sailed on HMS Beagle from England on 27 December 1831 as companion to Captain FitzRoy; voyage 1831 to 1836; On the Origin of Species, 1859.

title: Charles Darwin: The Beagle voyage
notes: Cited for: Darwin collected skulls, femurs and armour plates of giant ground sloths (such as Megatherium) in South America; Galapagos in September 1835; mockingbirds differed on four islands and were labeled by island, other birds (finches) were not.

title: Charles Darwin: Evolution by natural selection, the London years, 1836-42
notes: Cited for: John Gould diagnosed the Galapagos mockingbirds as three species unique to different islands (March 1837) and found the wrens, finches and gross-beaks were all ground finches; Darwin began asking how they diverged from mainland colonists.

title: Ionian revolt
