title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 5, chapter 105 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: Darius, told that Athenians and Ionians burned Sardis, ordered a servant to say "Master, remember the Athenians" three times whenever dinner was served.

title: Battle of Marathon
notes: Cited for: September 490 BCE on the Marathon plain; about 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans; Miltiades’ strong wings; Herodotus’s 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead; the runner to Sparta; the later legend.

title: Pheidippides
notes: Cited for: Herodotus records Pheidippides running from Athens to Sparta before Marathon; there is no record in Herodotus of a run from Marathon to Athens; the modern marathon honors the legend.

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 6, chapter 106 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: The Spartans told the Athenian messenger they could not march out until the moon was full.

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 6, chapter 120 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: After the full moon 2,000 Spartans reached Attica on the third day, too late for the battle; they viewed the dead at Marathon, praised the Athenians and went home.

title: Battle of Thermopylae
notes: Cited for: In 480 BCE about 7,000 Greeks under Leonidas held a line a few dozen yards wide for two days, then a smaller force held one more day; modern range for the Persian army of 70,000 to 300,000.

title: Battle of Thermopylae
notes: Cited for: Spartan king Leonidas; Ephialtes, a local from Trachis, showed the Persians the Anopaia path; Dieneces said they would fight in the shade.

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 7, chapter 186 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: Herodotus totals Xerxes’ fighting men at 2,641,610, more than 2.6 million.

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 7, chapter 226 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: Dieneces, told the Persian arrows would hide the sun, said the Greeks would then fight in the shade.

title: Battle of Salamis
notes: Cited for: In 480 BCE Themistocles lured a much larger Persian fleet into the narrow strait at Salamis; the Greeks sank about 300 Persian ships and lost about 40.

title: Themistocles
notes: Cited for: Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend a silver strike on the navy (200 triremes); evacuation of women and children to the Peloponnese; the false message to Xerxes.

title: Trireme
notes: Cited for: A trireme carried 170 oarsmen in three tiers and a bronze-clad ram.

title: Battle of Salamis
notes: Cited for: The Persians sacked Athens; much of its evacuated population sheltered on Salamis; the Greek victory at Plataea in 479 BCE ended Xerxes’ invasion.

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 8, chapter 90 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: Xerxes watched the battle of Salamis from the foot of the hill facing Salamis, with scribes recording who fought well.

title: Delian League
notes: Cited for: Founded 478 BCE against Persia; treasury in the temple of Apollo on Delos; Athens decided who gave ships or money; Naxos forced back; treasury moved to Athens in 454 BCE; disbanded in 404 BCE.

title: Delian League
notes: Cited for: Tribute built and maintained the fleet led by Athens; about 330 cities in the tribute lists; League funds partly paid for Pericles’ rebuilding, including the Parthenon.

title: Athenian Empire (course notes, CLAS 21)
notes: Cited for: Allies were converted from contributing ships to contributing cash, which left Athens with the power and the allies demilitarized.

title: Peloponnesian War
notes: Cited for: War of 431-404 BCE between Athens (Delian League) and Sparta (Peloponnesian League); Pericles’ strategy; plague; Sicily 415-413; Lysander, with Persian aid, destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405.

title: Thucydides on the Plague of Athens: Text & Commentary
notes: Cited for: The plague struck Athens in 430 BCE, crowded behind its walls on Pericles’ orders; it killed an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 people, including Pericles; Thucydides caught it and survived.

title: Thucydides, The Peloponnesian War, Book 1, chapter 23 (trans. Richard Crawley)
notes: Cited for: Thucydides names the growth of Athenian power and the alarm it caused in Sparta as the real cause of the war.

title: Xenophon, Hellenica, Book 2, chapter 2, section 23
notes: Cited for: After Athens surrendered, the Peloponnesians tore down its walls to the music of flute girls, thinking it the beginning of freedom for Greece.

title: The Tripod of Plataea (the Serpent Column)
publisher: Archaeological Site of Delphi, Hellenic Ministry of Culture
notes: Cited for: After Plataea in 479 BCE, 31 Greek cities dedicated a tripod on a bronze serpent column at Delphi; the Spartan commander Pausanias’s dedication was replaced by the cities’ names; Constantine moved the column to Constantinople, where it stands.

title: Constantinople, Hippodrome, Serpent Column
notes: Cited for: The Serpent Column lists the Lacedaemonians, Athenians and Corinthians first.

title: Mount Olympus
notes: Cited for: Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece (2,917 m, 9,570 feet), regarded as the home of the gods and the site of Zeus’s throne.

title: Who are some of the major figures of Greek mythology?
notes: Cited for: the 12 Olympians listed as Zeus, Hera, Aphrodite, Apollo, Ares, Artemis, Athena, Demeter, Dionysus, Hephaestus, Hermes and Poseidon, with Hades or Hestia sometimes included instead.

title: Greek religion
notes: Cited for: belief in many anthropomorphic deities under one supreme god; priests looked after cults, with no clergy and no sacred books.

title: Hestia
notes: Cited for: Hestia, goddess of the hearth, counted as one of the 12 Olympian deities.

title: Hera
notes: Cited for: Hera, queen of the Olympian gods and goddess of marriage; in literature the jealous, vindictive wife of Zeus who persecuted his loves.

title: Demeter
notes: Cited for: Demeter, goddess of agriculture and grain; Hades abducted her daughter Persephone; the pomegranate seed; the seasons.

title: Hermes
notes: Cited for: Hermes, divine messenger, protector of travelers and god of commerce and trade.

title: Hephaestus
notes: Cited for: Hephaestus, god of fire and a blacksmith who made weapons for the gods.

title: Zeus
notes: Cited for: Zeus, sky and weather god with the thunderbolt; Cronus swallowed his children; Rhea’s stone; Zeus hidden on Crete; the brothers’ victory over the Titans and division of the world.

title: Cronus
notes: Cited for: Cronus swallowed his children because he was warned a child would overthrow him; Rhea hid Zeus in Crete; Zeus forced Cronus to disgorge his siblings and won the war.

title: Cyclops
notes: Cited for: Hesiod’s Cyclopes Brontes, Steropes and Arges forged Zeus’s thunderbolt, Poseidon’s trident and Hades’ helmet of invisibility; Homer’s Polyphemus was Poseidon’s son.

title: Poseidon
notes: Cited for: Poseidon, god of the sea, earthquakes and horses; the trident; ’earth-shaker’; the sea fell to him by lot; lost Argos to Hera and flooded the land; delayed Odysseus’s homecoming.

title: Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.15.5 (trans. W. H. S. Jones)
notes: Cited for: the rivers judged the land of Argos to Hera, so Poseidon made their waters disappear; they give no water except after rain.

title: Athena
notes: Cited for: Athena, goddess of war, handicraft and practical reason; born fully armed from Zeus’s forehead; Metis; the owl; weaving; Medusa’s head on her aegis.

title: Apollo
notes: Cited for: Apollo and his twin Artemis born on Delos to Zeus and Leto; the bow and the lyre and what they stood for; prophecy and healing; Phoebus, ’bright’.

title: Hades
notes: Cited for: Hades, god of the underworld, the house of Hades; the underworld fell to him by lot; his name Pluto, ’Wealth’; Persephone his queen.

title: Charon
notes: Cited for: Charon ferried the souls of the buried dead over the Styx and Acheron, paid with the coin placed in the corpse’s mouth.

title: Cerberus
notes: Cited for: Cerberus, watchdog of the underworld, usually three-headed (50 heads in Hesiod), kept the living out and devoured escapers; Heracles fetched him.

title: Heracles
notes: Cited for: Heracles, son of Zeus and Alcmene, persecuted by Hera; the cradle serpents; the madness; serving Eurystheus; the twelve labors; his apotheosis.

title: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.12 (trans. J. G. Frazer)
notes: Cited for: the Pythian priestess told Heracles to dwell in Tiryns, serving Eurystheus for twelve years and performing ten labours, after which he would be immortal.

title: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.2 (trans. J. G. Frazer)
notes: Cited for: Eurystheus said the Hydra labour should not count among the ten because Heracles had the help of Iolaus.

title: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.5 (trans. J. G. Frazer)
notes: Cited for: Heracles cleaned Augeas’s cattle yard in a day by diverting the Alpheus and Peneus; Eurystheus would not count it because it was done for hire.

title: Perseus
notes: Cited for: Acrisius of Argos cast Perseus and Danae into the sea in a chest; Seriphus and Polydectes; the gifts; the shield reflection; Polydectes turned to stone; the discus; Perseus founded Mycenae.

title: Medusa
notes: Cited for: Medusa, the most famous Gorgon and the only mortal one, with snakes for hair and a gaze that turned people to stone; Pegasus sprang from her neck; Athena put the head on her aegis.

title: Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.16.3 (trans. W. H. S. Jones)
notes: Cited for: Perseus founded Mycenae, named after the cap (myces) of his scabbard that fell there, or, in another account, a mushroom (myces).

title: Theseus
notes: Cited for: Theseus, son of Aegeus king of Athens (or of Poseidon) and Aethra; the white and black sails; Aegeus’s death.

title: Aegeus
notes: Cited for: Aegeus, king of Athens and father of Theseus, drowned himself in the sea believing his son dead; the sea was thereafter called the Aegean.

title: Ariadne
notes: Cited for: Ariadne, daughter of Minos, helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth with a thread (or glittering jewels) after he killed the Minotaur.

title: clue (n.)
notes: Cited for: clue comes from clew, ’ball of thread’; the sense shift refers to Ariadne’s clew; spelling clue from the mid-15c.; figurative sense ’that which points the way’ from the 1620s.

title: Homer, Odyssey 9.360-414 (trans. A. T. Murray)
notes: Cited for: Odysseus tells Polyphemus his name is Noman; the blinded Cyclops cries that Noman is slaying him; the other Cyclopes tell him to pray to Poseidon and go away.

title: Siren
notes: Cited for: the Sirens, part bird and part woman, lured sailors to destruction with song; two in Homer; Odysseus stopped his crew’s ears with wax and was tied to the mast.

title: Scylla and Charybdis
notes: Cited for: two monsters on narrow waters no ship could pass without meeting one or both; Odysseus lost six men to Scylla; later localized in the Strait of Messina; the proverb.

title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 2, chapter 53 (trans. A. D. Godley)
notes: Cited for: Herodotus supposes Hesiod and Homer lived not more than 400 years before him and taught the Greeks the gods’ descent, names, spheres and forms.

title: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.15 (trans. R. Crawley)
notes: Cited for: before Theseus Attica was a set of independent townships; Theseus merged their councils into one at Athens; the state-paid Synoecia, or Feast of Union, dates from him.

title: Philosophy
notes: Cited for: the word philosophy comes from Greek philosophia, love of wisdom.

title: Pre-Socratic philosophy
notes: Cited for: the first Greek philosophers lived on the coast of Asia Minor (Ionia) in the 6th century BCE; Thales gave the first purely natural explanation of the world's origin.

title: Thales of Miletus
notes: Cited for: Thales' dates; water as the substance of all things; earth floating on water; his search for causes within nature rather than in the caprices of gods.

title: Thales of Miletus
notes: Cited for: Aristotle's report that Thales said water is the principle of things and his guesses why; Seneca's report of Thales' earthquake theory and its contrast with Poseidon; the well anecdote from Plato's Theaetetus.

title: Plato, Theaetetus 174a (trans. H. N. Fowler)
notes: Cited for: the story of Thales falling into a well while looking at the stars, mocked by a Thracian servant girl.

title: Xenophanes
notes: Cited for: Xenophanes' fragments on Homer and Hesiod, horses and oxen drawing gods, Ethiopians and Thracians, and his mockery of Pythagoras and the dog.

title: Anaximander
notes: Cited for: Anaximander, a pupil or associate of Thales, said everything came from the apeiron, the boundless.

title: Anaximenes of Miletus
notes: Cited for: Anaximenes chose air as the basic substance, which condenses into cloud, water, earth and stone and rarefies into fire.

title: Pythagoras
notes: Cited for: Pythagoras on Samos and his move to Croton about 530 BCE; the five-year silence in later tradition; no books; the bean taboo; the musical ratios 2:1, 3:2, 4:3; Xenophanes' puppy story.

title: Pythagoras
notes: Cited for: Pythagorean rules (no beans, barefoot in temples, white clothing); belief that souls are reborn in animals, so all life is kin; numbers in the world and in music.

title: Pythagorean theorem
notes: Cited for: Babylonian tablets from about 1900-1600 BCE show knowledge of the theorem; doubt that Pythagoras proved it.

title: Socrates
notes: Cited for: Socrates' dates; he wrote nothing and is known mainly through Plato and Xenophon; the oracle and his questioning of politicians, poets and craftsmen; the charges, accusers, conviction and hemlock; suspicion over Critias.

title: Socrates
notes: Cited for: the elenchus; the trial and its context, including Critias and the Thirty.

title: Plato, Apology (trans. H. N. Fowler)
notes: Cited for: Chaerephon and the oracle (21a); Socrates wiser in not thinking he knows what he does not (21d); the gadfly (30e); thirty votes (36a); meals in the prytaneum (36d).

title: Plato's Shorter Ethical Works
notes: Cited for: the Laches' definitions of courage (staying at your post; endurance of the soul), Socrates' objections, and the dialogue's ending without an answer.

title: Cicero, Tusculanae Disputationes 5.10 (ed. M. Pohlenz)
notes: Cited for: Cicero's remark that Socrates first called philosophy down from the heavens into cities and homes, to ask about life, morals, good and evil.

title: Thirty Tyrants
notes: Cited for: the Thirty, led by Critias, ruled Athens in 404-403 BCE after its defeat in the Peloponnesian War.

title: Plato: Phaedo
notes: Cited for: the Phaedo's account of Socrates' death, with numbness rising from his legs to his heart.

title: Plato
notes: Cited for: Plato's dates; student of Socrates; the Socratic dialogues; the Academy founded in the 380s BCE; the Forms, such as Justice, Beauty and Equality.

title: Plato: The Academy
notes: Cited for: the Akademeia outside the walls of Athens; Aristotle's 20 years there (367-347 BCE).

title: academy (n.)
notes: Cited for: English academy comes from Greek Akademeia, the grove where Plato taught.

title: Plato, Republic 7.514a (trans. Paul Shorey)
notes: Cited for: the allegory of the cave (514a-517a): prisoners, fire, shadows, the ascent to sunlight, and the prisoners' threat to kill whoever frees them.

title: Plato's Allegory of the Cave: the Journey Out of Ignorance
notes: Cited for: the prisoners' threat to kill the liberator read as a reference to Socrates' execution; the sun as the Form of the Good.

title: Aristotle
notes: Cited for: born 384 BCE at Stagira; 20 years at the Academy from 367; back in Athens in 335; the range of his subjects; more than 500 species; studies on Lesbos; fish stories proved right centuries later; his criticism of the Forms.

title: Aristotle
notes: Cited for: the Lyceum and the name Peripatetics; the first logic; perhaps 200 treatises, about 31 surviving, which read like lecture notes.

title: Aristotle's Ethics
notes: Cited for: the doctrine of the mean; courage between cowardice and rashness.

title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1096a (trans. H. Rackham)
notes: Cited for: both friends and truth are dear, but it is our duty to prefer the truth.

title: Stoicism
notes: Cited for: Stoicism founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens about 300 BCE, named for the Stoa Poikile; virtue the only good; passions as errors of judgment; Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.

title: Zeno of Citium
notes: Cited for: Zeno came to Athens about 312 BCE, studied with Crates the Cynic and taught in the Stoa Poikile.

title: Epicurus
notes: Cited for: dates; the Garden, about 306 BCE, open to women and slaves; pleasure as absence of pain in body and trouble in soul; barley bread and water.

title: Epicurus
notes: Cited for: the Garden; aponia and ataraxia; death is nothing to us.

title: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book X (trans. R. D. Hicks)
notes: Cited for: Epicurus' letter asking for a little pot of cheese so he could feast.

title: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI: Diogenes (trans. R. D. Hicks)
notes: Cited for: Diogenes' exile, jar, lamp ("I am looking for a man"), plucked fowl, Alexander ("Stand out of my light") and "citizen of the world".

title: Diogenes
notes: Cited for: Diogenes of Sinope, archetype of the Cynics; poverty and begging; the tradition of the search for an honest man with a lantern.

title: Cynics
notes: Cited for: the name Cynic from kynikos, dog-like, probably from Diogenes' public life; Crates as his pupil and Zeno as Crates' pupil; kosmopolites.

title: Euclid
notes: Cited for: Euclid flourished about 300 BCE in Alexandria; Book I opens with 23 definitions, five postulates and five common notions; the Elements was compiled from earlier works, but its design was his own; the 'no royal road' story.

title: Elements (work by Euclid)
notes: Cited for: the Elements has 13 books (plane geometry, number theory, solid geometry); set a standard for deductive reasoning and geometry teaching for more than 2,000 years.

title: Euclid of Alexandria (MacTutor History of Mathematics)
publisher: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
notes: Cited for: more than 1,000 editions of the Elements since its first printing in 1482; Proclus reports the 'no royal road' story; 13 books.

title: Euclid's Elements, Book I (D. E. Joyce)
notes: Cited for: Book I has 23 definitions, 5 postulates and 5 common notions; Definition 1, 'A point is that which has no part.'

title: Archimedes
notes: Cited for: dates and Syracuse; law of the lever; On Floating Bodies; wreath story probably true, bath and 'Eureka' embellishment; killed in the sack of Syracuse; tomb with sphere and cylinder; Plutarch on practical inventions; Sand-Reckoner describes Aristarchus's system.

title: The Golden Crown (Chris Rorres, Archimedes pages)
publisher: Courant Institute, New York University (Chris Rorres)
notes: Cited for: Vitruvius, a Roman architect of the 1st century BCE, tells how Archimedes tested King Hiero II's gold crown for silver.

title: Archimedes' Lever (Chris Rorres, Archimedes pages)
publisher: Courant Institute, New York University (Chris Rorres)
notes: Cited for: 'Give me a place to stand on, and I will move the earth' is quoted by Pappus of Alexandria, Synagoge Book VIII, about 340 CE.

title: Archimedes of Syracuse (MacTutor History of Mathematics)
publisher: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
notes: Cited for: killed by a Roman soldier when Syracuse fell; Plutarch says he regarded engineering as ignoble; Cicero found his tomb with a sphere and cylinder.

title: Eratosthenes of Cyrene (MacTutor History of Mathematics)
publisher: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
notes: Cited for: the nicknames Beta and Pentathlos (second-best across many fields); librarian at Alexandria; assumed the Sun's rays are parallel; 250,000 stadia.

title: Eratosthenes (Ancient Astronomy, UNLV Physics and Astronomy, D. Jeffery)
notes: Cited for: Eratosthenes assumed parallel sunlight; by Euclid's geometry of parallel lines, the Sun's angle from vertical at Alexandria equals the angle at Earth's center between Alexandria and Syene.

title: Eudoxus of Cnidus
notes: Cited for: 27 geo-concentric spheres (one for the stars, three each for Sun and Moon, four for each planet); Aristotle endorsed the model; uniform circular motion remained orthodox until Kepler.

title: Hipparchus
notes: Cited for: catalog of about 850 stars; found precession by comparing his observations with 5th- and 3rd-century BCE observations (a shift of about 2 degrees); Ptolemy relied on his work.

title: Antikythera Mechanism (Return to Antikythera, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution)
notes: Cited for: found by sponge divers in 1901; the most sophisticated mechanism surviving from antiquity; nothing as complex for a thousand years after the fall of Rome.

title: Hippocrates
notes: Cited for: born about 460 BCE on Cos, died about 375 BCE; known from Plato as an admired physician and teacher; about 60 writings bear his name, most not by him; case histories, diagnosis and prognosis.

title: On the Sacred Disease, by Hippocrates, translated by Francis Adams (The Internet Classics Archive)
notes: Cited for: the disease called sacred is 'nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause'; the brain is its cause; those who called it sacred used the gods as a screen for their inability.

title: Humor (ancient physiology)
notes: Cited for: the four humors, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile; health as the right mixture; theory still current in the European Middle Ages.

title: On the Nature of Man, from the Hippocratic Corpus (HIST 139, Carleton College)
notes: Cited for: the Hippocratic On the Nature of Man, about 400 BCE, explained illness as an imbalance of the four humors.

title: Hippocratic oath
notes: Cited for: the oath dates to about 400 BCE; sworn by Apollo and other gods; beneficial treatment and confidentiality; revised versions still used at many medical school graduations.

title: Democritus
notes: Cited for: born about 460 BCE, citizen of Abdera, pupil of Leucippus; atoms indivisible, moving in the void, differing in shape, arrangement, position and size; qualities exist by convention; Aristotle rejected atomism.

title: Democritus (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
notes: Cited for: Aristotle's letter comparison (A and N, AN and NA, N and Z); the 'by convention sweet... in reality atoms and void' fragment; atoms too small to perceive.

title: Eratosthenes' Geography (Roller), book description
notes: Cited for: Eratosthenes invented the discipline of geography and probably the word geographia; a grid of parallels and meridians; some 400 places from Thoule to Taprobane.

title: Collection Highlight: Ptolemy's Geographia Universalis (University of Rochester River Campus Libraries)
publisher: University of Rochester River Campus Libraries
notes: Cited for: the Geography gives longitudes and latitudes of around 8,000 places; Latin translation completed 1406 to 1409; its grid of longitude and latitude gave Renaissance mapmakers a framework.

title: Ctesibius of Alexandria
notes: Cited for: flourished about 270 BCE; improved water clock with a float and pointer; force pumps; water organ.

title: Heron of Alexandria
notes: Cited for: flourished about 62 CE; the aeolipile, a steam-spun sphere, the first steam-powered engine, used for toys and to amuse; Pneumatica describes coin-operated machines, singing birds and a fire engine.

title: Theatre of Dionysus
notes: Cited for: on the south side of the Acropolis; site of the contests where Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were first performed; the annual spring festival of the god.

title: Theatre (building)
notes: Cited for: theatron means a place of seeing; the orchestra was the circular dancing place; actors dressed in the skene, then a small tent, source of scene; the holy image carried in so the god could be present; admission free at first, later poor citizens given entrance money.

title: Ancient Greek Theatre
notes: Cited for: all performers male, masks; up to three actors; tragic chorus of up to 15 who sang and danced; each poet submitted three tragedies and a satyr play; a panel judged; Thespis and the word thespian.

title: Greek Theatre Architecture
notes: Cited for: theatres evolved from a stage area set before a natural hill on which spectators sat.

title: Ancient Theatre of Epidavros
notes: Cited for: built in the late 4th century BCE on the west side of Mount Cynortion; regarded as the most perfect Greek theatre for acoustics; the Epidaurus Festival stages ancient drama each summer.

title: Tragedy (literature)
notes: Cited for: tragedy from tragoidia, goat-song; Aeschylus added a second speaker; about 90 plays attributed to Aeschylus, seven survive.

title: Aeschylus
notes: Cited for: added a second actor; about 90 plays, seven tragedies survive complete; Oresteia (458 BCE) the only surviving complete trilogy.

title: Sophocles
notes: Cited for: about 123 plays, seven survive; introduced the third actor; perhaps as many as 24 victories against 4 for Euripides.

title: Euripides
notes: Cited for: 92 plays known, 19 extant counting one disputed; only four first prizes; his fame later eclipsed Aeschylus and Sophocles, so more of his plays survive.

title: Oresteia
notes: Cited for: first performed 458 BCE; the only complete Greek trilogy to survive; Agamemnon returns from the Trojan War and is murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra.

title: Ancient Greek Tragedy
notes: Cited for: the plot of a tragedy was almost always inspired by episodes from Greek mythology.

title: Classical Drama and Society, Chapter 7: Classical Greek Tragedy, Part 2
notes: Cited for: audiences knew the general outline of a myth but never knew which version a playwright would stage.

title: Aristophanes
notes: Cited for: about 40 plays, 11 survive; Old Comedy of satire and political criticism; Knights (424 BCE) attacks Cleon; Clouds (423 BCE) satirizes Socrates.

title: Lysistrata
notes: Cited for: produced 411 BCE; Athenian and Spartan women refuse sex until the men end the Peloponnesian War.

title: The Frogs
notes: Cited for: first prize at the Lenaea in 405 BCE; Dionysus goes to the underworld, judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides and chooses Aeschylus.

title: Menander
notes: Cited for: about 342 to 292 BCE; greatest poet of New Comedy; over 100 plays; everyday situations and stock characters; texts lost until papyrus finds in Egypt; Dyskolos first printed in 1958.

title: Aulos
notes: Cited for: a reed pipe played in pairs in the Classical period, one in each hand; players wore a leather strap (phorbeia) across the cheeks.

title: Lyre
notes: Cited for: arms and a crossbar; the chelys made from a tortoise shell; Hermes made the lyre from a tortoise shell and gave it to Apollo over the stolen cattle; the lyre accompanied singing and poetry and was integral to Greek education.

title: Aulos
notes: Cited for: the aulos accompanied male choruses and played at the theatre, in worship of Dionysus, at athletic contests and at drinking parties.

title: Homer, Odyssey 8.62ff.
notes: Cited for: the blind minstrel Demodocus, his lyre hung on a peg, sings of the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles at the Phaeacian feast, and Odysseus hides his tears.

title: Lyric
notes: Cited for: lyric derives from the lyre, which accompanied Greek lyric poetry; it expresses personal emotion; monodic (Sappho, Alcaeus) and choral (Pindar) lyric.

title: Sappho
notes: Cited for: about 610 to 570 BCE, Lesbos; love, desire, weddings and her circle of women; admired for her style; nine books edited in Alexandria, lost by the early Middle Ages; one complete poem, the ode to Aphrodite.

title: Guide to the classics: Sappho, a poet in fragments
notes: Cited for: fragments from Oxyrhynchus, an ancient garbage dump in Egypt, and from mummy cartonnage; the 2004 old-age poem; new fragments in 2013; called the Tenth Muse.

title: Roman Copies of Greek Statues
notes: Cited for: many works now known only in Roman marble copies were first made in bronze; marble copies needed supports, often carved as tree trunks. (Page blocked automated fetch; content confirmed via search excerpt.)

title: Riace Bronzes
notes: Cited for: two Greek bronze warriors, probably mid-5th century BCE, found in the sea off Riace, southern Italy, in 1972; among the few surviving full-size Greek bronzes, which were usually melted down.

title: Krater
notes: Cited for: an ancient Greek vessel used for diluting wine with water.

title: Competing for olive oil: a Panathenaic prize amphora
notes: Cited for: prize amphorae full of olive oil; black-figure kept long after other pottery dropped it; Athena on one side, the contest on the other.

title: Vitruvius, On Architecture, Book IV

notes: Cited for: Peri's La Dafne (1598), probably the first opera; L'Euridice (1600), the first opera whose music survives complete; dramatic singing unlike Renaissance polyphony.

title: La favola d'Orfeo
notes: Cited for: Monteverdi's Orfeo first performed at Mantua in 1607 with about 40 instruments; first time a composer specified the instruments; first opera to keep a place in the modern repertory.

title: Recitative
notes: Cited for: recitative imitates the rhythms and accents of speech, using few pitches, and carries dialogue and plot, while the aria carries emotion.

title: San Cassiano Theatre
notes: Cited for: Europe's first public opera house, opened in Venice in 1637, taking opera beyond royal and noble patronage.

title: Jean-Baptiste Lully
notes: Cited for: Lully's royal appointments under Louis XIV; he died (1687) of an infected foot wound caused by his long conducting stick.

title: Conductor (music)
notes: Cited for: in Bach's and Handel's time the composer led from organ or harpsichord; concertmaster led at the Paris Opera; a conductor stresses the pulse so all follow the same meter and cues entries.

title: Mannheim school
notes: Cited for: the Mannheim orchestra famous for disciplined virtuosity, long crescendos; Burney's 'army of generals'; significant role in the Classical symphony.

title: Symphony
notes: Cited for: symphony as a lengthy orchestral work in several movements; typical Classical four movements (fast, slow, minuet, fast finale); origin in the Italian opera overture (fast-slow-fast sinfonia); continuo abandoned after about 1770.

title: Who was the first conductor? When did they start using batons?
notes: Cited for: no widespread use of batons until around 1820, when Louis Spohr brought the practice from Germany to London; music grew more complex and orchestras larger from the early 19th century.

title: Joseph Haydn
notes: Cited for: Haydn's dates (1732-1809); appointed by the Esterhazy family in 1761 and served nearly 30 years; the Farewell Symphony No. 45.

title: What you should know about Joseph Haydn
notes: Cited for: Haydn as Father of the Symphony and of the String Quartet; isolated at Eszterhaza, 'forced to become original'; Farewell Symphony at the prince's summer palace.

title: Symphony No. 45, "Farewell", Joseph Haydn
notes: Cited for: in 1772 the homesick musicians wanted to go home; in the finale player after player blew out his candle and left; the prince gave them leave.

title: "Father of the Symphony": Haydn's Musical Legacy
notes: Cited for: Haydn wrote 104 symphonies, which gave later composers a symphonic template.

title: Minuet
notes: Cited for: the minuet as an elegant couple dance in moderate triple time (3/4); typically the third movement of a Classical symphony or string quartet.

title: Surprise Symphony
notes: Cited for: Haydn's Symphony No. 94, premiered in London on March 23, 1792, named for a startlingly loud chord in the soft second movement.

title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
notes: Cited for: Mozart's dates and places; chords at three, pieces at four, composing at five; tours with Leopold and Nannerl; more than 600 works; Figaro, Don Giovanni, The Magic Flute; Requiem completed by Sussmayr.

title: Antonio Salieri
notes: Cited for: no foundation for the belief that Salieri poisoned Mozart; Pushkin (1830) and Shaffer's Amadeus (filmed 1984); Salieri's pupils Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt.

title: Mozart's music does not make you smarter, study finds
notes: Cited for: the 1993 finding of better spatial-task performance by college students after Mozart; the 2010 meta-analysis of about 40 studies and over 3,000 participants found no support for a Mozart-specific gain.

title: Chamber music
notes: Cited for: string quartet of two violins, viola and cello; one player to a part and usually no conductor; development owed largely to Haydn; principal chamber medium from about 1750.

title: The Cambridge Companion to the String Quartet (sample chapter)
publisher: Cambridge University Press (via Library of Congress catalog samples)
notes: Cited for: the Classical quartet as an intimate dialogue among equals, challenging to play; Haydn's Op. 33 and Mozart's quartets dedicated to Haydn as the prototype; Goethe's 'four rational people conversing'.

title: Mozart and Haydn in Vienna
notes: Cited for: Haydn and Mozart played quartets together in the 1780s (Haydn violin, Mozart viola); Mozart dedicated six quartets to Haydn in 1785, an unusual honor; Haydn's praise of Mozart to Leopold.

title: Western music: The Classical period
notes: Cited for: Classical style's simplicity and clarity of form; homophonic, melody-dominated texture as a reaction against late-Baroque polyphony.

title: Ludwig van Beethoven
notes: Cited for: baptized in Bonn 17 December 1770; left for Vienna in autumn 1792 to study with Haydn; buzzing and lost high notes before 1800; died Vienna 26 March 1827; predominant figure between the Classical and Romantic eras.

title: Eroica Symphony
notes: Cited for: planned dedication to Napoleon; Napoleon named emperor December 1804; Beethoven tore the title page; premiere Vienna 7 April 1805; grander than customary; a symphony presenting its creator's image of the world.

title: Symphony No. 5 in C Minor, Op. 67
notes: Cited for: opening of three Gs and a sustained E-flat; C minor with a finale in C major; premiere Vienna 22 December 1808.

title: Symphony No. 9 in D Minor, Op. 125
notes: Cited for: premiere Vienna 7 May 1824; finale with chorus and soloists on Schiller's Ode to Joy; Beethoven profoundly deaf; Umlauf led; a singer turned him to see the applause.

title: Heard with Beethoven's ear
notes: Cited for: the documented progression of Beethoven's hearing loss: 1801 letters, high notes and tinnitus, ear trumpets around 1814-1815, conversation books from 1818, composing with his inner ear.

title: Conversation books (archive glossary)
notes: Cited for: Beethoven used conversation books from 1818 to communicate with visitors, who wrote while he usually answered aloud.

title: Beethoven's complete Heiligenstadt Testament
notes: Cited for: text of the Heiligenstadt Testament (October 1802) to his brothers: hiding his deafness, being thought unfriendly, only art held him back from ending his life.

title: Program music
notes: Cited for: program music is instrumental music carrying an extramusical program (literary idea, legend, scene or personal drama); absolute music is its opposite; Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830) with printed program.

title: Hector Berlioz
notes: Cited for: Symphonie fantastique finished and performed in 1830; its recurring theme, the idee fixe; love from a distance for the actress Harriet Smithson.

title: Berlioz: Symphonie fantastique (program note)
notes: Cited for: premiere 5 December 1830 in Paris with a printed program; the beloved becomes a melody, the idee fixe, grotesquely transformed in the witches' sabbath; Berlioz married Harriet Smithson in 1833.

title: Frederic Chopin
notes: Cited for: born 1 March 1810 near Warsaw; left Poland in 1830; Paris from 1831; wrote little but piano works; mazurkas and polonaises from nationalist feeling; delicate touch suited to intimate settings; died 17 October 1849 aged 39; heart in Holy Cross Church, Warsaw; friend of Liszt.

title: Mazurka
notes: Cited for: Polish folk dance for couples with stamping and heel clicks; 3/4 or 3/8 time with a strong accent on the second beat; Chopin wrote about 57 mazurkas.

title: Rubato
notes: Cited for: rubato, from Italian rubare, to rob: stretching some beats and compacting others for expression.

title: Rubato: a guide to the musical term meaning 'robbed time'
notes: Cited for: Chopin's rubato kept the tempo fairly steady in the left hand while bending it in the right.

title: Niccolo Paganini
notes: Cited for: born Genoa 1782; 24 Caprices (1801-1807) with harmonics and pizzicato; rumors of a pact with the devil and of prison for murder; sensational Paris and London appearances 1831; 1832 British tour made him wealthy; immense influence on Liszt.

title: Franz Liszt
notes: Cited for: born 1811 in the kingdom of Hungary; resolved to transfer Paganini's violin effects to the piano after hearing him; first to give complete solo piano recitals.

title: How Franz Liszt invented the piano recital
notes: Cited for: Liszt's 1840 London concerts advertised as 'Liszt's Pianoforte Recitals', the first musical use of 'recital', previously used for dramatic readings.

title: Lisztomania: why did women go gaga for 19th century pianist Franz Liszt?
publisher: The Conversation (Timothy McKenry, Australian Catholic University)
notes: Cited for: Heinrich Heine coined 'Lisztomania' in 1844; period drawings show women swooning and flowers thrown at the stage.

title: Giuseppe Verdi
notes: Cited for: born 1813; Un giorno di regno failed and Nabucco (1842) succeeded, making him at 28 the new hero of Italian music; Va, pensiero became an unofficial national anthem; literary sources; Rigoletto 1851, La traviata 1853, Aida 1871, Otello 1887, Falstaff 1893; died 1901.

title: Falstaff (opera by Verdi)
notes: Cited for: Falstaff premiered at La Scala in 1893, from Shakespeare; Verdi's only other comedy had failed there half a century earlier.

title: Giuseppe Verdi: Uniting Italy With Music
notes: Cited for: historians debate whether the link between Verdi's music and nationalism formed more gradually than often claimed; Aida debuted in Egypt in 1871.

title: Timeline: Viva Verdi
notes: Cited for: at the 1901 procession moving Verdi's remains in Milan, a choir of 820 voices led by Toscanini sang Va, pensiero.

title: Richard Wagner
notes: Cited for: born Leipzig 1813; music drama as poetic drama in a continuous vocal-symphonic texture; leitmotifs; the Ring's four operas, first complete at Bayreuth in 1876; section on his antisemitism (Judaism in Music, 1850; Hitler; unofficial ban in Israel; disputed legacy).

title: Festival History: Origins at a Glance
notes: Cited for: the Festspielhaus built to Wagner's design opened on 13 August 1876 with the complete Ring; the orchestra hidden beneath the stage, the 'invisible' orchestra.

title: A beginner's guide to Wagner's Ring cycle
notes: Cited for: the Ring's four operas total about 15 hours of music.

title: Nationalistic music
notes: Cited for: nationalism in Romantic music drew on folk tunes, folk dances, folklore and village life; leaders included Smetana and Dvorak (Czech), Grieg (Norway), Glinka (Russia).

title: Bedrich Smetana
notes: Cited for: founder of the Czech national school; totally deaf in late 1874, then wrote the six symphonic poems of Ma vlast (1874-1879).

title: The Moldau
notes: Cited for: the Vltava from its source in the Bohemian Forest through the countryside (hunters, a village wedding in polka rhythm) to Prague; completed 1874; second of the six parts of Ma vlast.

title: Finlandia
notes: Cited for: composed 1899 for the Press Pension Celebration, a veiled rally for press freedom in Finland under tsarist Russia; originally called 'Finland Awakes'.

title: Sibelius: Finlandia (program note)
notes: Cited for: to avoid Russian censorship some early performances used neutral titles such as Impromptu or Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring.

title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
notes: Cited for: born 1840 in Votkinsk; died 1893 in St. Petersburg; Swan Lake (1877), The Sleeping Beauty, The Nutcracker (1892).

title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Is Staged in St. Petersburg (Research Starters)
notes: Cited for: the 1877 Bolshoi premiere was poorly received, the music rejected as too dramatic and emotional, like Wagner's dark style; Tchaikovsky died in 1893; the 1895 Mariinsky restaging by Petipa and Ivanov is the version most followed today.

title: The Nutcracker
notes: Cited for: premiered December 1892 at the Mariinsky Theatre, St. Petersburg; Tchaikovsky heard the celesta as the voice of the Sugar Plum Fairy and wrote to his publisher to acquire one.

title: The Secret Story Behind Tchaikovsky's Mysterious Celesta in The Nutcracker
notes: Cited for: Tchaikovsky found the celesta in Paris, described it as between a piano and a glockenspiel, and asked his publisher for secrecy lest Rimsky-Korsakov or Glazunov use it first.

title: What's on the Golden Record
notes: Cited for: launched in 1977, both Voyagers carry the Golden Record into interstellar space; contents chosen by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan; an eclectic 90-minute selection of music.

title: Golden Record Sounds and Music
notes: Cited for: the list of music on the Voyager record, including Java court gamelan, Senegal percussion, Kesarbai Kerkar's raga, Goro Yamaguchi's shakuhachi, Bach and Chuck Berry.

title: Ethnomusicology
notes: Cited for: ethnomusicology as the study of all world musics; the term introduced around 1950 by Jaap Kunst and American scholars, replacing comparative musicology; dependence on field research.

title: Mission and History
notes: Cited for: Moses Asch founded Folkways Records in 1948 to document people's music and sounds from around the world; the Smithsonian acquired it in 1987.

title: African music
notes: Cited for: polyrhythm and timeline patterns on bells as key features; Yoruba dundun talking drums with oriki praise poetry; griots as troubadour-historians.

title: Tala
notes: Cited for: tala as a metric cycle of a fixed number of beats with no exact Western equivalent; Hindustani and Carnatic talas; tintal 16 beats; claps and waves; patterns that contradict the tala then return.

title: Gamelan
notes: Cited for: the orchestra of Java and Bali, largely gongs and tuned metal instruments struck with mallets; each gamelan tuned to itself; slendro and pelog.

title: Raga
notes: Cited for: raga as a set of notes with a typical order and characteristic motifs; several hundred in use; northern classification by mood, season and time of day; improvisation within the raga's tones.

title: Hindustani music
notes: Cited for: one of the two principal types of South Asian classical music, in the north; performances over an hour opening with the nonmetric alap; tambura drone, tabla and sitar.

title: Listening to Solo Tabla
notes: Cited for: the sam, the first beat of the tala cycle, is its point of maximum rhythmic resolution.

title: Javanese Gamelan
notes: Cited for: Central Javanese gamelan instruments and functions; gong ageng marking the gongan; slendro and pelog as a double set; pelog pieces built on five-note sets; performance contexts.

title: Agbadza: The Critical Edition
notes: Cited for: Agbadza as the main music and dance of the Ewe; the 2+2+1+2+2+2+1 bell time line; the recurring bell phrase keeps polyrhythmic alignment; sogo, kidi, kagan, gankogui, axatse, handclaps.

title: Talking drum
notes: Cited for: talking drums imitate the rhythm and rise and fall of words; Yoruba dundun pressure drums and Asante atumpan.

title: Talking Drum
notes: Cited for: the talking drum as an hourglass-shaped pressure drum with cords between its heads, squeezed under the arm to change pitch; imitating tonal languages, proverbs and praise songs.

title: Griot
notes: Cited for: griots (jeli or jali in Mande languages) as hereditary West African troubadour-historians who preserve genealogies and oral traditions; advisers and diplomats; many play the 21-string kora.

title: Kora
notes: Cited for: the kora as a long-necked harp lute with 21 strings and a calabash gourd resonator.

title: Kora: in search of the origins of west Africa's famed stringed musical instrument
notes: Cited for: a jeli (called a griot by outsiders) is a hereditary oral historian and musician; the kora has 21 strings and is played with four fingers.

title: Oud
notes: Cited for: the oud's deep pear-shaped body, fretless fingerboard and short neck; four pairs of strings classical; plucked with a plectrum; name from Arabic 'ud, wood; parent of the European lute; present form probably from Andalusia.

title: Lute (definition and etymology)
notes: Cited for: English 'lute' comes through French and Old Occitan from Arabic al-'ud, literally 'the wood'.

title: Maqam
notes: Cited for: maqam as a set of pitches, characteristic motifs and a traditional pattern of use; three-quarter and five-quarter tones; about 50 maqamat; taqsim; roughly related to the Indian raga.

title: Erhu
notes: Cited for: the erhu as a bowed two-stringed Chinese vertical fiddle, strings a fifth apart over a snakeskin-covered resonator, no fingerboard, held upright on the thigh.

title: Sihu
notes: Cited for: the bow hairs of huqin fiddles such as the erhu pass between the strings.

title: Koto
notes: Cited for: the koto as a long Japanese board zither with 13 strings and movable bridges, plucked with tsume picks; related to the Chinese zheng; long known as Japan's national instrument.

title: Shakuhachi
notes: Cited for: the shakuhachi as a Japanese end-blown bamboo flute derived from the Chinese xiao in the 8th century, with four finger holes and a thumbhole; name from its length, one shaku eight sun.

title: Shakuhachi: The History and Practice of Suizen
publisher: Japan House, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
notes: Cited for: Edo-period Fuke Zen komuso ('monks of emptiness') playing shakuhachi in public in straw-woven basket hats; suizen, 'blowing Zen'.

title: Flamenco
notes: Cited for: cante as the essence of flamenco and cante jondo; golden age about 1780-1845; cafes cantantes from 1842; dance dominant since the mid-19th century; arm, hand, footwork and heelwork.

title: Flamenco
notes: Cited for: inscribed 2010; fusion of cante, baile and toque; Andalusia as heartland; the Gitano (Roma) community's essential role; seated cante with no backing singers; toque has surpassed accompaniment; handclapping, foot-stamping, castanets.

title: The flamenco compas analogy
notes: Cited for: the compas as the 12-beat measure into which triplets and doublets are arranged and accented, coordinating singers, instrumentalists and dancers.

title: The Flamenco Key: Phrygian Mode, Andalucian Cadence, and Cambios
publisher: University of California San Diego (John Moore)
notes: Cited for: soleares as a fundamental flamenco form performed in a slow twelve-beat pattern and considered cante jondo.

title: Samba de Roda of the Reconcavo of Bahia
notes: Cited for: samba de roda developed in Bahia's Reconcavo in the 17th century, drawing heavily on the traditions of enslaved Africans; the roda circle; migrants took it to Rio, influencing urban samba.

title: Tango
notes: Cited for: tango evolved about 1880 in Buenos Aires, merging the Spanish tango (a variety of flamenco) with the milonga, possibly the habanera; a European craze by 1915; melancholy by 1920.

title: Tango
notes: Cited for: tango developed by urban lower classes in Buenos Aires and Montevideo, mixing European immigrants, descendants of African slaves and criollos.

title: Salsa
notes: Cited for: salsa ('sauce') as a hybrid based on Afro-Cuban music and the Cuban son; development in New York with Puerto Rican musicians Tito Puente and Eddie Palmieri; Celia Cruz; 1970s peak.

title: Braiding Rhythms: The Role of Bell Patterns in West African and Afro-Caribbean Music
notes: Cited for: clave as two wooden sticks and the pattern they play, the foundation of Afro-Cuban music; polyrhythmic traditions followed Africans to the Caribbean through the slave trade; the Ghanaian 'Gome' pattern would be called son clave.

title: Folk music
notes: Cited for: folk music as traditional, generally rural music passed down through families and small groups; lives in oral tradition, learned by hearing; transmission and variation.

title: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, 1666 N.S.
notes: Cited for: Pepys's January 1666 entry on hearing Mrs. Knipp sing 'her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen'.

title: Song of the Week: Barbara Allen
publisher: Library of Congress, American Folklife Center (Folklife Today)
notes: Cited for: Barbara Allen (Child 84) as one of the ballads most collected by fieldworkers, in many names and versions; Charles Seeger's 1966 Library of Congress LP Versions and Variants of the Tunes of Barbara Allen.

title: Cecil Sharp
notes: Cited for: Cecil Sharp and Maud Karpeles spent 46 weeks in Southern Appalachian communities between 1916 and 1918, collecting songs of English origin and distinctly American ones.

title: Introduction - African American Spirituals: Resources in the American Folklife Center
notes: Cited for: spirituals as religious folksongs created and sung by enslaved people of African descent in the American South; oral transmission; call-and-response between leader and chorus; clapping and patting.

title: Work song
notes: Cited for: work songs keep a regular rhythm for a task; during and after slavery Black American workers developed spirituals and, ultimately, the blues out of older work song traditions.

title: Work Song, Field Call & More (Timeline of African American Music)
notes: Cited for: work songs passed the time and coordinated workers; song leaders improvised a line and others answered with a refrain.

title: Let My People Go: Moses in African American Spirituals
publisher: St. Olaf College, Music 345: Race, Identity, and Representation in American Music
notes: Cited for: "Go Down, Moses" and the Exodus story; the refrain "let my people go"; Moses songs reflect enslaved people's longing for freedom.

title: Go Down, Moses
notes: Cited for: "Go Down, Moses" originated in the slave community of the southern US, adopts the Exodus story to express the desire for freedom; call-and-response with the congregation singing "Let my people go!".

title: Fisk Jubilee Singers
notes: Cited for: Fisk established in 1865 to educate formerly enslaved people; in debt by 1871; choir formed to raise money; 1873 European tour and Queen Victoria; Jubilee Hall built from tour proceeds; spirituals rarely heard outside Black churches or homes.

title: Blues
notes: Cited for: blues as secular folk music created by African Americans in the South after the Civil War; AAB three-line stanza; 12-measure form on tonic, subdominant and dominant; bent blue notes.

title: Rural/Folk Blues (Timeline of African American Music)
notes: Cited for: blues recognizable in the Deep South in the 1890s; roots in work songs, field calls, spirituals and ballads; AAB stanza; 12-bar form on three chords; guitarists bend strings or slide a bottleneck to emphasize blue notes.

title: Blue note
notes: Cited for: blue note as a microtonal lowering of the third, seventh and sometimes fifth degrees of the major scale.

title: W.C. Handy Encounters the Blues
notes: Cited for: around 1903 at the Tutwiler train station, Handy heard a man playing guitar with a knife pressed on the strings and singing; Handy became known as the Father of the Blues.

title: W.C. Handy
notes: Cited for: Handy's 'The Memphis Blues' (published 1912) and 'St. Louis Blues' (1914); autobiography Father of the Blues.

title: Ragtime
notes: Cited for: ragtime as the predominant American popular style from about 1899 to 1917 and a forerunner of jazz; steady left hand against syncopated right hand; banjo styles and cakewalk rhythms; Maple Leaf Rag 1899; Joplin as King of Ragtime.

title: Ragtime (Timeline of African American Music)
notes: Cited for: to 'rag' a piece was to syncopate its melody; left hand on the beats, right hand syncopated; Joplin the best-known ragtime composer; Maple Leaf Rag (1899).

title: Scott Joplin
notes: Cited for: Joplin born 1867/68 in Texas, died 1917; 'king of ragtime'; Treemonisha published at his own expense in 1911; 1970s revival through The Sting; posthumous special Pulitzer Prize in 1976.

title: The Magical 'Maple Leaf Rag'
notes: Cited for: Maple Leaf Rag became the signature piece of ragtime and helped set the foundations for jazz. (Its '75,000 copies in six months' sales figure is disputed and is not used.)

title: Scott Joplin
notes: Cited for: 1976 special award, bestowed posthumously in the Bicentennial Year, for Joplin's contributions to American music.

title: Jazz Origins in New Orleans
publisher: New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park (National Park Service)
notes: Cited for: Congo Square Sunday gatherings of enslaved people; brass bands and cultural mix; 1890s segregation laws uniting Black and Creole of color musicians; Bolden 1895-1900; collective improvisation; 1917 first commercial jazz recording.

title: Charles "Buddy" Bolden
publisher: New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park (National Park Service)
notes: Cited for: Bolden's cornet band generally considered the first to play what became jazz; horn said to be heard miles away; no recording was ever made.

title: A New Orleans Jazz History, 1895-1927
publisher: New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park (National Park Service)
notes: Cited for: front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone over guitar, bass and drums; wartime Chicago boom meant jobs for musicians; Oliver in Chicago; Armstrong joined in 1922; Hot Five from 1925.

title: Jazz
notes: Cited for: jazz developed by African Americans, influenced by European harmonic structure and African rhythms; rhythmic and structural elements mainly from West African traditions, instruments like trumpet and trombone from Europe.

title: The First Jazz Recording Was Made by a Group of White Guys?
notes: Cited for: Original Dixieland Jass Band, five white musicians, recorded 'Livery Stable Blues' on February 26, 1917, likely the first jazz recording issued; jazz as an expression of African American culture.

title: Louis Armstrong
notes: Cited for: born 1901 in New Orleans; learned cornet at the Colored Waifs Home (1913); joined Oliver in Chicago 1922; Hot Five and Hot Seven 1925-28, first great jazz soloist; 'West End Blues' (1928); one of the inventors of scat singing; influenced virtually all later jazz horn players.

title: Louis Armstrong Education Kit, Act 4: Innovative Trumpeter, 1925-1929
publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
notes: Cited for: Hot Five and Hot Seven departed from collective improvising and focused on the break, so the soloist was the star; recordings made in Chicago 1925-1928; scat as wordless phrases; 'Heebie Jeebies' among the earliest scat recordings.

title: Swing
notes: Cited for: swing era about 1935 to the mid-1940s; sections of brass, woodwinds and rhythm played off against each other; swing as momentum from attack and accent against fixed beats; Fletcher Henderson's 1920s bands; lindy hop.

title: Benny Goodman
notes: Cited for: 'King of Swing'; Henderson's charts gave the band its most characteristic sound; hired Teddy Wilson despite fearing the consequences, then Lionel Hampton (1936); integration gave Black musicians visibility during segregation.

title: Duke Ellington
notes: Cited for: born 1899 in Washington, D.C., died 1974; Cotton Club residencies from 1927; led his band for more than half a century; composed thousands of scores and works to highlight his soloists; 'Mood Indigo' (1930) for muted trumpet, unmuted trombone and low-register clarinet.

title: Duke Ellington at the Smithsonian
notes: Cited for: short score for 'Mood Indigo' (1930) in the NMAH Duke Ellington Collection labels lines for specific players: 'Barney' (Barney Bigard), 'Tizol' (Juan Tizol), 'Tricky' (Joe 'Tricky Sam' Nanton).

title: Cotton Club
notes: Cited for: Harlem nightspot that featured Black entertainers but limited its audience to white patrons; Ellington's orchestra hired as house band in 1927.

title: Duke Ellington
notes: Cited for: 1999 special citation in recognition of Ellington's musical genius, which evoked aesthetically the principles of democracy through the medium of jazz.

title: Bebop (Timeline of African American Music)
notes: Cited for: bebop evolved out of and in reaction to the swing bands; jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem; Gillespie, Parker, Monk, Clarke; rapid tempos, lines based on harmony, small combos; shift from dance music to listening.

title: Bebop
notes: Cited for: bebop originated in the early 1940s; Gillespie, Parker, Monk, Clarke, Christian; substituted chords superimposed on older harmonies; initially unacceptable to the public and many musicians.

title: "Ko Ko" -- Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, Dizzy Gillespie, and others (1945)
publisher: Library of Congress, National Recording Preservation Board
notes: Cited for: Parker's December 1939 epiphany jamming on 'Cherokee' (higher intervals such as 9th, 11th, 13th); 'Cherokee' is 64 measures and challenged jazz musicians 1938-1945; 'Ko Ko' (recorded 1945) uses its chord structure with the theme omitted; added to the National Recording Registry in 2002.

title: What is Jazz?
publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
notes: Cited for: in most jazz performances players play solos they make up on the spot; improvising over a chord progression; swing and blue notes; call-and-response between instruments, voices or parts of the band; making a familiar tune fresh and personal.

title: Improvisation
notes: Cited for: improvisation survives as one of the chief distinguishing characteristics of jazz, structured by a model such as a well-known show tune.

title: Great Migration
notes: Cited for: an estimated six million Black people moved from the rural South to Northern and Western cities (1916-1970), escaping Jim Crow laws and sharecropping; racism rampant in the North too; migrants changed the sound of the blues they brought north.

title: Physicist revives oldest recording of the human voice
publisher: symmetry magazine (Fermilab and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory)
notes: Cited for: Scott de Martinville's 1860 phonautograph recording of Au Clair de la Lune on soot-covered paper, never meant for playback; Carl Haber (Berkeley Lab) played it back in March 2008.

title: Phonautograms: Edouard-Leon Scott de Martinville (c. 1853-1861)
publisher: Library of Congress, National Recording Preservation Board
notes: Cited for: phonautograph inscribed airborne sound on paper to be studied visually, not played back; the phonautograms are in the National Recording Registry.

title: Origins of Sound Recording: Thomas Edison
publisher: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
notes: Cited for: Edison's 1877 phonograph was the first machine to both record sounds and play them back; first test was Mary Had a Little Lamb.

title: Phonograph
notes: Cited for: tinfoil phonograph mechanism (diaphragm and needlelike stylus pressing pits into tinfoil; lighter stylus traces pits for playback; hand-cranked cylinder).

title: Tinfoil Phonograph
publisher: Thomas A. Edison Papers, Rutgers University
notes: Cited for: tinfoil wrapped around a hand-cranked grooved cylinder; Edison recorded Mary Had a Little Lamb as his first test.

title: KDKA
